lore: The rule on that road is old and worth keeping. Build shelves out of it. Build a counter, a door, a bench for the fire. Do not build a bed. Whatever it eventually takes into its head to do, you want to be standing up when it does it.

dark_iron_quills.description: A cluster of grey spines, hard as nails and about as friendly. Tuskmaul wears a ridge of them.

lore.t: Nothing about them is a quill. They are the grey spines off the ridge of a
Tuskmaul

, a hand long, hard enough to pin oak, and the name comes from one man at one fire who split a tip, dipped it, and produced a blot the size of his thumb and a line that gave out after two letters. He has not been allowed to forget it.

lore: He is also the reason four fires on that road can read at all. He taught it evenings, for nothing, badly, for about sixty years, and when he comes in for a drink now somebody always sets an inkpot down in front of him, and he always looks at it, and everybody laughs, himself included and loudest.
Thirty gold the cluster. Joiners buy them, not scribes. Iron weeps in that country and a quill never has.

dark_red_star_stone.description: Near-black, veined dark red around a red star at the core, out of a Rotjaw. It will not let you go down either.

lore.t: Forty-two gold: the cheapest useful stone in the country, for the one service no seller has ever managed to price honestly. The arithmetic behind the discount is not pretty.
The animal

stands where the hill tracks begin to climb, it does not run, and it will still be standing there next season. Common is the whole of the reason. Every bag-carrier on the hill roads has one and most of them have never found out whether it works.

lore: It is near-black, veined dark red under the surface like something that has not gone out, with a small red star at the middle brighter than any part of a stone should be. It fires once. A blow that was going to put you down does not, and you are on your feet with nothing left but the standing, and the beat you have been handed is short and yours to do something with. People it has happened to report the same odd thing afterwards, never the one you expect. Not that they survived. That the end arrived and then declined to become the next moment.

lore.t: Jehanne

keeps a bowl of them inside her door and puts one into the hand of anyone leaving her fire for a road, and takes nothing for it. She does not promise them it works. She does not tell them it will not. She has been carrying out a practice she stopped believing in for longer than most of them have been in the world, and the only defence of the bowl she has ever offered is that a forty-gold stone is at least a thing you can put in somebody's hand.

dark_teal_plate_stone.description: Dark teal plates, always beaded with water. The thing that grew it has not surfaced yet.
lore: Grading is comparison. You hold the stone against the creature — that is the entire method, and it works, because one kind of creature leaves one kind of stone and the trade has spent a long time pairing them off. There is nothing to hold this one against. So the graders read it backwards instead, out of what it does, and every one of them arrives at the same sentence and none of them enjoy saying it aloud: whatever reached the bottom of this had no particular reason to come up.

It is heavy for its size and plated like something's back, overlapping dark teal with a bright seam at every edge, warm as any stone in the trade and beaded all over with water it has no business having. Worn, you swim like a thing that lives down there. And you breathe. Not hold your breath longer — breathe, for as long as you care to, which is the part sellers say twice.

lore.t: Gunnar

uses one for work. A Turn put four miles of the low road under water eleven years ago and he has walked the whole of it since, along the bottom, correcting a map he has not been asked for. He has said one thing about the stone, to one person, and it had nothing to do with the map: down there he does not think about breathing at all, and twice he has come up only because the light went, and he could not afterwards say how long he had been under. He does not speculate about what grew it. He has noticed what it does to a man only borrowing the habit, and he has gone back down anyway.

dead_red_leaf.description: One leaf gone crimson out of season. Thornstag browses a branch and the whole branch ends up like this.

lore.t: A
Thornstag

leaves a line of them behind it, crimson in a green month, plain as chalk on a wall, and any fool can read it. Any fool does. What the line gives you is where the animal has been, which is the half of the question nobody was asking. The other half — where it is going — is sold by four or five people who get it by sitting out an autumn night near something worth robbing. The colour keeps for years, which is the second trade in them: a red leaf is the cheapest way to prove to a fire that you have been somewhere.

deep_red_crack_stone.description: Deep red plates with every crack lit orange to a hot centre. Whatever it came out of has not been brought down yet.
lore: Every other stone on a bench is in the past tense. A stone is what is left when a shape comes apart; the shape is accounted for, the creature is a matter of record, and the whole vocabulary runs that way — released, cracked, brought in. This one is sold with a tense the trade does not otherwise use. Not yet, said flatly, the way you would say a thing about scheduling.

A hundred gold, and not a fighting stone. Against anything still whole it does nothing worth the setting; against something already opened it adds twelve and hands you back a twentieth. The graders go this far and no further, and they say it as a description of the stone and of nothing else: what reached the bottom here was not hunger and was not endurance. It was a preference for things that had already begun to lose.

lore.t: Then the arithmetic, which everybody does once and drops. Nineteen have come in that anyone can put a name to.
One kind of creature, one kind of stone

— so nineteen stones are nineteen shapes broken, by hands, at some hour, in some country, and not one of those hands has ever sat down at a fire and said so. Either it is being done quietly, which is not how crackers are; a good story is half the wage. Or the first rule anybody learns has a hole in it the exact size of this stone.

dented_metal_flask.description: A traveller's flask, dented flat on one side. Empty, but it still smells faintly of something strong.

lore.t: Everything else that comes down off a
Nightmule

is work — rope, harness links, canvas, a knife for rations. The flask is the only thing in that load that was not about getting somewhere. It is dented flat down one whole side and the cap still seats, so it took the blow while it was full and did not lose a drop, which is a good flask, and the man who owned it knew that about it.
Wendell

is clear on what the object is for. Nobody carries a flask to drink by himself, he says. You carry it so that at the end of a wet day you have something to hand across, and the handing is the point and the drink is only the excuse. He says this at a fire, in exchange for company, which is a man describing his own method and trusting you not to notice. Twenty-five gold, and he has never once been asked for a demonstration.

dried_grass_bundle.description: Olive stalks tied off with cord, dry to the heart. Fodder, thatch, bedding — and the best tinder on the road.
lore: Ask three people what it is for and get fodder, thatch and bedding. Ask anyone who keeps a fire and get one answer. A twist of it rides inside the coat, against the body, where it stays dry through whatever the sky is doing; it comes out last, it goes under the kindling, and it is the difference between a lit hearth at dusk and a cold one.

lore.t: There is a girl on one of the western rotas — one of the few
still kept

— who let hers get wet at a ford and walked four hours back for another twist rather than come in and say so. She was fourteen when she died. She has kept that fire ninety years and she is still fourteen, and the walk back is what the other keepers tell about her, in the tone people use for somebody they intend to be proud of forever.

ember_starburst_stone.description: Dark red with an orange star bursting through the cracks. Cinderhowl is cracked open the same way.
lore: Every hard piece comes out warm. This one comes out hot at the middle and stays there, so it travels in a tin, lashed to the outside of the pack. Every dealer says so to every new buyer, and every second one finds out the other way regardless. There are men on the west road who will show you the hole in the lining before you have asked.

lore.t: Most of them go to
the rotas

rather than to the fights. A keeper on a wet round can shove one under sodden kindling, walk off to see to somebody, and come back to a fire. It does not want dry, or shelter, or nursing, and it will do it again tomorrow night and in four hundred years, and seventy-two gold for that is not a price, it is a gift. Half the western keepers who still hold a rota worth the name have one, and treat it exactly like a kettle.
What the people who fetch them will not do is set one in a blade.
The hound

leaves its work still going on behind it, embers putting themselves out in the grass a long while after it has gone by, and a stone is the bottom of the kind, so that is what you have bought: the hit lands, and then it goes on landing, while you stand there. The trade rests on two words and both of them describe one blow. Ask a cracker why he keeps his in a tin and you get a shrug, or you get the honest answer, which is that he does not want to be given the time to change his mind.

engraved_bronze_locket.description: Oval bronze, knotted over with spirals, a ring at the top for a cord. It is a locket. It has never once opened.
lore: Opening it is the first thing everybody tries and the last thing anybody manages. Some have a hinge line under the knotwork and some have no hinge line whatsoever, and all of them are shut, and the trade has been quiet about that for a long while, on the grounds that eighty-five gold is a fair price and the question is not worth losing over.

lore.t: Two facts sit side by side in
the Chronicle
with no third fact between them. They come up in the grass where
Runemane
walks. And they come off the black rock, grown in under the chest skin of a
Palehusk
— a thing with nothing at all inside it, carrying, over the exact place a heart would sit, a container that has never been opened.

fen_bloom_stone.description: Green stone cracked with pale light, off a Mireback. Mushrooms fruit on it if you leave it alone.
lore: Shut one in a bag for a week and there are pinheads in the seams. Leave it a month and they are red-caps, small and entirely ordinary, fruiting on a mineral that has no business feeding anything. Wipe them off and they come again. Nothing else out of a broken shape does this, and most sellers polish before a viewing and say nothing about it, which is how the dyed ones got as far as they did.

For the better part of a decade a man worked the fen circuit with pale stones soaked green, priced a third under, and a story about the swamp being poor ground to collect in. He was right about the ground. Three buyers worked out what they had and told their fires, and it went on anyway, because the fakes showed better than the true ones — brighter, cleaner, nothing rotting in the seams.

lore.t: It ended over a bag. A dealer asked to see the bag and not the stone, and the bag was clean, and every honest
Mireback
stone stains its cloth. That is the grading now: you are not buying the stone, you are buying the mark it left on the lining.

lore: What it pays out is not protection. The work comes back to you as fast as you do it, and comes back double standing in water. A wood bear whose wood went four feet under did not stop walking its round when the ground changed its mind. Neither does the piece at the bottom of it.

flame_veined_shard.description: Leaf-shaped crystal veined orange and red. It stays warm in the pouch, like the shell it was prised from.
lore: Blood heat, near enough, and it keeps it for years. That makes it the one piece of junk with an obvious use and no cleverness required: it goes in a pocket, and the pocket is warm.

lore.t: Jehanne

buys them by the sack every autumn — the cracked and cloudy ones, which is why she can afford sacks — and hands them out on the winter rounds to whoever is sitting up at a fire with no one else on the rota. She says nothing over them. She has nothing to say over them. An old man at the third fire thanked her last year for the blessing, and she stood a moment, and then told him he was welcome, because correcting him would have cost him something and saved her nothing at all.

fossil_oyster_shell.description: One half of a fossil bivalve, chalk on the outside, pearly within. The dunes are full of dead seas.

lore.t: They come up as halves. A woman on the south dune camps spent two years looking for the other half of hers — not a similar one, the one, hinge-notch and all — and she went at it properly: every shell and flake that came in off a
delver
's wake laid against her own on a folded cloth, a tally kept, a small fee paid for the privilege of looking.

lore: She found one that fitted. It was not the mate; the chalk was wrong and the size a shade under. It closed anyway, and sat closed in her hand, and she stopped that evening and has not started again. She still buys shells off anyone coming in off the sand. She does not lay them against anything now. She says she likes the noise they make in the bag.

fresh_green_herbs.description: A fistful of green stalks pulled up roots and all, tied at the base by somebody in a hurry.

lore.t: There is a pot on at every fire worth the name, and this is most of what goes in it: whatever came up green within a short walk, pulled roots and all, tied with whatever the picker had on them. Nobody arrives hungry. That is not what the pot is for. It is for the hour after
a waking

, when a person has been told what has happened to them, and asked their name, and cannot produce it yet, and needs something to do with their hands while they try. One man got as far as saying his mother put nettles in everything and it made the whole house smell like a wet field. That was his one true thing. His name came back three days later, and of the two it was much the smaller.

frost_rimed_claw.description: A blue-grey claw with rime still on the edge. Bergclaw leaves them in shields, mostly other people's.

lore.t: Lay one flat and the curve very nearly closes on itself. That is not a claw for opening a thing — that is a hook, and a hook is for holding on. Shields that come back with one in them come back with the boards pulled rather than scored: the arm took hold and leaned, and whoever was behind it had about a second to decide whether to keep the shield. They almost all keep it.
Osric

has re-boarded eight in two years and keeps the claws in a jar on the sill, still cold, still rimed, sweating a ring into the wood. He offers them back and is told no every time, by people who cannot say why either. He has stopped asking. He has not thrown one out.

frost_star_crystal.description: A six-armed crystal that never quite melts. Winterfang's mane grows them and drops them behind it.
lore: Never quite is the whole of it. A dropped star loses a hair's width a year and no more, so a trail of them is a trail with dates on it: big ones from this winter, smaller from the winter before, back and back until you are reading a line the animal walked a century ago and can still put your thumb on.

lore.t: Gunnar

measures those lines, because they are the only straight thing this country hands out free. He has one off the north fells, eighty stars long, and the far half of it does not lie where the near half points. The ground under it moved. He wrote the numbers down and has shown them to no one, and when
Winterfang
comes up at a fire he talks about the cold instead.

furred_dark_claw.description: One dark claw with the fur still on the knuckle. It came off a paw the size of a dinner plate.

lore.t: Two things in the west leave a claw this size, and only one of them ever grew hair. Scrape the knuckle: coarse brown, flattened all one way, skin still on underneath. That is
Mireback
, which was an ordinary bear on ordinary ground before the water came up over its round. The other kind leaves grit and green crumbs and no hair at all, because
Cragback
was never an animal — it is a hill a hundred valleys agreed on, and hills do not grow coats.

lore: Buyers on the west road pay double for hair. It is not a better claw — same socket, same edge. What the extra gold buys is the certainty that the paw had a bear inside it once, which matters enormously to some people and not at all to others, and both sorts drink at the same fire and gave up arguing about it years ago.

gilded_curved_fang.description: Someone gilded a hunter's tooth, hollow at the root and polished bright. Nobody asks whose mouth it left.

lore.t: The leaf costs more than the tooth under it, and that is the exercise, not an accident of taste.
Gold

is the one substance every century remembers the same way, which is why a coin holds while everything around it goes soft, and there are people who reason from that fact straight to this practice: lay enough of it over a thing and the thing comes along for the ride. It has never been properly tested. It is done anyway, and it is not done to wedding rings or lucky coins. It is done to teeth. This one went over a
Duskfang

's, out of an age so far back it has stopped coming up at the fires at all — which is the part worth sitting with, because gilding is what a person does about a creature when they have run out of anybody willing to talk about it. Seventy-two gold, and most of that is the gold.

glossy_brown_seeds.description: Hard glossy kernels streaked tan and brown, a good fistful. Small woodland things hoard them, and now so do you.
lore: Hard as a knuckle. There are two ways to open one — a flat stone, or your own back teeth — and which a person reaches for tells you how long they have been here.

lore.t: The newly woken

protect their teeth. They will not say why, and the reason is a chair in a bright room and a mother who was firm about it. Everyone else cracks them on the molars without a thought, because a tooth here is a remembered tooth and behaves like the rest of you. The first time somebody hears their own jaw go through a shell and feels nothing whatever about it, they generally go quiet for the rest of the evening, and the fire lets them, and somebody moves the bowl within reach. Five gold the fistful. That is the cost of the fistful, and it is not the price.

glowing_ember_dust.description: A handful of grit that still glows in the palm. Cinderhowl leaves a trail of it wherever it walks.

lore.t: Twenty-four gold the twist, and there is one reason for the price: a pinch of it under wet kindling gives you a fire when nothing else in the pack will. In the rain country that is not a convenience. A night with no fire is a night with no telling in it, and the walkers up there buy by the tin. The woman who supplies most of the west road quotes all of that back at you while she weighs, and she has her own arithmetic. She works after dark, a hundred paces behind
the burning dog

, sweeping the grit out of the ruts before it goes out — twelve years of it, one road, both directions. Every fire between the ford and the high fields is lit off her sweepings. She has never sat at one.

gnarled_mandrake_root.description: A knobbly root with legs of its own and a wilted crown. The Stumpling was carrying it, or it was family.

lore.t: Forty gold for a root off a
Stumpling

's foot, and every coin of it is the shape. The stalls grade them the way a fishmonger grades fish. Two legs is a root. Two legs and arms is a good root. A head — a knob with a fold in it, the light doing the rest — is a price you have to ask about, quietly, and the seller takes his time answering.

lore: It sells as a joke. They hang it by the crown with a scrap of coat on it and do the voice, and the crowd obliges. It is bought in earnest far more often than the stalls admit, by people careful to be laughing while they pay. There is a right way to sell a man a root shaped like a small person: take his gold, make the joke, wrap it well, and do not watch him leave.

gold_seamed_teal_soulstone.description: Sea-green, webbed with gold where it broke and broke again. It holds armour together, and gold has a way of turning up.
lore: Gold in the hand is always cold. The gold in this one is exactly as warm as the sea-green around it, and that detail still stops conversations. The mend is no setting, either: it runs the whole way through, filed and worked like trade goldwork, and it will not come out of the stone, nor the stone off it.

Handlers grade by the seams and argue the count — one school calls it a tally of seasons worked, the other says a stone is not a calendar. What the count means is not argued: this broke, and held, and broke again, and held. Armourers promise only that a plate carrying one comes apart later than it should, and often not at all. A stone that is mostly mend teaches a mend.

lore.t: Halvard
, the pedlar who walks his pack between the fires and
prices in nothing but gold
, will buy one, sell one, carry one — and book it as stone, never as gold: gold that cannot be spent is not gold to him. Pressed once, he weighed a
Palemaw

stone in his palm, said the difference between the two prices was the animal, and would not be drawn further. He does allow that carriers find more gold in a season than luck explains, and he counts his purse twice after trading with one.

gold_sunburst_rune_stone.description: Gold-cased and cut with a sunburst rune, left by a Runemane. It is still carrying out old orders.
lore: The two who brought the first one in could not agree, that night at the fire, on what they had done. One of them used the polite word and said released. The other would not take either of the trade's two words and kept saying, instead, that they had taken a fitting off a building.

lore.t: He had the better of it and everybody knew.
The guardian

is Made: it never fell and was never anywhere, only remembering that pooled with nothing to be, thickened, and stood up at a door. A stone is the last hard piece of somebody, the bottom of a long forgetting, and there is not supposed to be a bottom to a thing that was never filled. Yet here it lies in its gold case, warm as any of them, the sunburst still lit in the cut of it, doing what it plainly does: set it in a blade and every fifth strike, unasked and without fail, it puts itself in front of the next blow. It is not protecting you. It is standing where it was told to stand.
They left it at the meadow fire and went, which is what people do with a thing they cannot price.
Solveig

has had it in her apron since. Somebody there made the obvious comparison out loud, in the tone people use when they think they are being kind — the last one on a rota that lapsed everywhere else. She said the lion was left with orders and she was left with people, and that these are not the same thing, and got up to see to the wood.

gold_veined_ore.description: Rubble-grade rock studded with raw gold. It was a Mosscairn's shoulder until you argued about ownership.
lore: The first thing a new cracker is taught about ore is how to be disappointed properly. Teeth are no use on rock. You drag a fleck across a pale stone and read the line it leaves — true gold draws yellow, the pretty fraud draws black — and then you heft the lump, because a fist of real ore weighs like a bigger stone than it looks.

lore.t: The second thing is that
Halvard
pays under weight for it, always, and will not be moved.
A coin is the one thing everyone remembers the same

; a rock with gold in it is a rock with an argument in it, and he does not trade in arguments. Melt it and come back, he says. Half the sheds think he is squeezing them. The other half has noticed he pays exactly the same under-weight to the people he likes.

golden_broad_fang.description: Broad amber-yellow tooth, split from crown to root. Even an Emberjaw loses one on the wrong kind of bone.
lore: It split crown to root, and it split from closing, not from being struck. A tooth that comes apart the long way did it to itself, biting down on something that would not open.

lore.t: Which is why there is a list, and the list is the whole conversation every time one of these crosses a counter.
Ironhide
's plates. The black glass out of the volcano. Whatever it is a
Palemaw

keeps working on ground where nothing else will feed. Three, and everyone agrees on the three, and then the counting runs on a beat too long, and somebody buys the fang, and the talk goes somewhere else.

lore: Thirty gold. Amber ivory takes a shine like nothing else in the trade, and half the buyers do not care about any of the above, which is a mercy on the ones who do.

great_curved_fang.description: A fang as long as a hand, worn blunt at the tip. Tuskmaul has broken plenty on other people's shields.

lore.t: Buyers want them blunt, and the reasoning is not sentiment. A fang worn round at the point has been in service a long time, which means the animal carrying it is old and settled and accounted for, standing where it has stood since before anyone thought to look — the way
the old bull
stands. A sharp one has come off something that has not finished growing.

lore: So the blunt fetches thirty-two gold and the sharp fetches half, and the difference has nothing to do with ivory. It is the arithmetic. Somewhere in country that everybody has agreed for two hundred years is empty, on ground people cross without looking up, there is a new one. The man who brings a sharp fang to a counter is asked where he found it, politely, immediately, and by everybody in the room at once.

green_crystal_shard.description: Teal-green crystal with a wicked point, prised out of a Mosscairn's seams. Holds an edge and a grudge.
lore: The grudge is a shop joke. A hafted jade point keeps its edge past all reason — past the steel beside it on the bench, past the arm using it — and when a cutler cannot explain a thing he gives it a temper instead. So the shards are surly, the good ones are spiteful, and everybody laughs.

lore.t: An apprentice at the sheds asked, in front of the whole bench, whether a piece off a
Mosscairn

remembers having been part of one. The bench laughed. The master did not. He let it go all afternoon, and then, while the boy was sweeping up, said without turning round that they do not ask that in here, and went back to work.

green_emerald_cluster.description: Deep green and sharply faceted, prised out of stubborn rock. Mosscairn keeps them in its shoulders.

lore.t: Beautiful and structurally useless. Emerald is full of its own flaws and every one of them is a line waiting to be asked a question; set it in a blade and the first honest blow finds one.
Sigrun

will take your money for the work and tell you plainly where it is going: handle, never head. A stone in the head takes every blow you strike for as long as you own the thing. A stone in the handle takes only what your own hand gives it. She has never once elaborated on the distinction, and the apprentices who have looked closely at the head of her hammer have never asked her to.

green_herb_bundle.description: Long green stalks tied into a sheaf, damp from the ditch some blob had been squatting in.
lore: Nine people at one fire, nine names for it, every one of them certain. Marsh-tongue. Ditch-sorrel. Goosegrass, poor-man's-bay, the one the drovers call cutfinger, and a Latin one from a man who was a physician for thirty years and has not been one for four hundred. They agreed on exactly two things: boil it, and it is good with fish.

lore.t: Bettany

wrote down all nine, which annoyed the entire fire, since eight of them are obviously wrong. She will not choose. Her position, stated once and never repeated, is that a plant nine people remember nine ways is a plant nine people are holding up, and
the book
is not in the business of taking eight of them away. The stall on that road sells it under the name everyone actually uses, which is bundle.

green_jewel_beetle.description: A beetle in green and blue enamel, legs folded neat. Too handsome to squash, and in no position to object.

lore.t: The shell does not dull and does not fade, which makes it the brooch of anybody who cannot afford a brooch. Pinned at the throat it reads as enamel from four feet, and only the very rude look closer.
Osric

bought one last spring for a birthday, which is a thing almost nobody here keeps any more — he still counts in living years and marks the date the way he marked it before. He was two months out. He gave it anyway, and it is being worn.

green_ooze_glob.description: A palmful of green ooze that keeps its shape and none of its dignity. Alchemists take it by the jar.

lore.t: Sold by the jar, and the jar is the argument.
Seven gold

buys a jar of it, so the only thing left to haggle over is whose jar, and every buyer on the fen road keeps one that is a finger taller than everybody else's and swears it is the standard. There is a woman working the low crossings with her own on a strap, fired to a scratched line she put there herself, who will not pour into anything but that. She has been called a great deal at that counter. She has also never once been short-paid, so half the crossing brings her their globs now and lets her do the pouring, and she takes nothing for it. She is not doing it for them. She is doing it at him.

green_scale_cluster.description: A patch of overlapping green scales, still faintly damp. Palemaw sheds them in the cave shallows.

lore.t: There is a shelter at the last fire before the black rock: four stone walls roofed in green scale, a handful at a time, over years. Everybody who works that ground adds to it on the way out. Overlapped right, the scales throw rain off like slate and never crack in the heat coming off the rock, and they never dry either — the ceiling is damp all night, which is the only complaint anyone makes. Twelve gold a patch and hundreds up there: the roof is worth more than the shelter and the woodpile together, and it has never been stripped. Not sentiment. Anybody stripping it would have to carry it out past the men who put it up, and they are all coming back the same way, off
Palemaw
's ground, in a hurry.

green_slime_glob.description: Half a pond-dweller, domed and translucent, still faintly warm. Alchemists want it and will not say why.

lore.t: Boiled two hours it goes down to a thin green size that holds paper to paper and does not turn brittle, and that is what
Bettany
binds
the Chronicle
with. Every account of the worst day of somebody's life that she has ever taken down is held into the spine by eight gold of pond-dweller off a fen stall.

lore: She explained this once, at the stall, in detail, being a scribe and unable to help it. The price was eleven inside the month. She has explained nothing at a market since, buys by the sack now, and lets the road go on believing she is one of the alchemists — which is cheaper, and, she admits, a better story than the truth.

green_slit_eyeball.description: A green eye with a black slit, still bright. Mireglare's stare stays in it about an hour, then goes out.
lore: It is the one thing on the stall you can price by looking at it. Bright, twenty-eight. Dull, eight. The hour in between is the entire difference, so sellers come off the crossing at a trot with the bag held level and quote you the time they cut it.

lore.t: A walker out of the low ford keeps one long past its hour, flat and grey now, in a pouch he does not sell out of.
The cat that comes into firelight

looked him over one night — the whole way, chin up, as you are supposed to let it — and then moved on to the next face and out into the dark. He has had a good many years to decide whether being passed over is the good outcome and has not managed it. He keeps the eye because he would like to be able to ask it.

green_venom_vein_stone.description: Cobbled grey plates, green standing wet in every joint. In a blade the poison layers on and never clears out.
lore: It travels alone, at the bottom of the bag, with something folded between it and the rest, because the green gets out — not much, never fast, never stopping. A pouch that has carried one for a season is marked inside for good. The crackers' rule is flat: you carry one of these, or you carry the rest.

lore.t: So somebody has to walk the green bag, and the somebody is
Jehanne

. She took the office unasked, the way she takes every office no one else wants, and walks a day behind the buying party with the bag on a pole over her shoulder, washing her hands at every stream, saying over each stone the blessing of a faith she tells everyone she no longer holds. The trade pays her in firewood. She has never once been robbed.
Graders can usually say inside a minute whether the thing in their hand is a fact, an appetite, or a habit. This one is none of the three. It is a substance — the same green
the Palehusk
leaks — and a substance is not a life pressed small. It grades high anyway. High enough that the question rarely gets asked twice.

grey_grindstone.description: Grey-brown and split by dark seams, ground smooth. Gnashjaw wears its tusks down on rock like this.

lore.t: Osric

has patched the same coat of mail three times for the same customer and finally said it across the counter: it is not cutting your mail, it is using it. A stone like this does not hit hard. It takes a little armour off, hands it back a breath later, takes a little more — and a man carrying one who simply keeps coming at you all afternoon will have the whole coat by evening. Forty-five gold. Every second beginner owns one, and the few who learn patience early keep it for years.
Go and watch
Gnashjaw

and you will see an animal filing its own tusks flat on a boulder, and you will call it tooth-care, because that is what it looks like and because the other reading takes some sitting with. The stone will not leave you the comfortable one. Pale grey lobes in rust-dark seams, the whole face worn flat and glossy, warm in the hand: what refused to thin any further in that creature was not the teeth, and was not the strength either. It was the wearing away. An animal can keep what its life is about to itself for as long as you care to stand there looking at it. A stone cannot, and every dealer between here and the east country has held one, and the young ones are out there grinding tonight.

grey_rock_pile.description: Rounded brown stones in a heap, which is all a Mosscairn amounts to once it stops holding itself together.

lore.t: Three. Not three each — three for the heap, and the heap weighs about what you do. So the money in rubble is not in the taking, it is in the carrying, and behind every crew there are men who have never
opened a shape

in their lives and make a steady living hauling other people's stone to the weighing-post at the road. There is one on the east road who has done it forty years. To anyone who calls it a poor trade he points out that he is paid per stone the same as the man who took it, sleeps a good deal better, and has never in all that time carried anything off a hillside except the weight.

grey_sage_leaves.description: Bitter grey-green leaves off the meadow scrub. Good in stew, better in a poultice, and a handful will put you down.

lore.t: The women who sell it count the leaves into your hand out loud. That is not ceremony. Three in a pot of stew is a good dinner. A dozen crushed into a wet rag is the best thing going for a bad shoulder. A fistful, chewed, and you go down — properly down, on your face, in the road — and come back together beside the nearest fire some hours later,
the way anyone does
, pockets intact, a hole where your evening was, and a little less of whatever you had been thinking about.

lore: One man worked that out and made a habit of it. Pleasant, paid without haggling, back every few weeks and lighter each time. The trade argued about him for a winter and came out with a rule it keeps still: they will sell you your fistful. They will not sell you the second, they will not say who might, and every woman on that road knows his face.

grey_stone_crimson_veins.description: Cold grey plates with a warm red seam shut inside them. It gives nothing until you cut, and then it takes its share back.
lore: Buyers turn one to the light, hunting the gap where the red shows through. The crackers gave that habit up years ago — shut tight or on show, it is the same stone — and test with the fist instead: close it and wait for one warm line to come up against the palm, in a stone otherwise colder than the grass it came out of.

What it does begins half a breath after your first cut lands. Whatever you opened, some part of it comes back the other way and closes what it finds. Everyone who has felt it says the same two things in the same order: that it is a great deal of comfort, and that it is not a kindness. Nothing is being given. Something is being taken and divided.

lore.t: Gunnar
wears one wired in behind his belt buckle on the far rounds, through country the
Duskfang
still holds. Asked at the meadow fire what carrying it is like, he gave the question thought — which from Gunnar is a long answer already — and said: like being lent to. He did not say by whom.

grey_violet_charge_stone.description: Grey stone veined in dead violet, off a Gravecharger. It is still trying to reach a line that fell centuries ago.
lore: It pays nothing to a man standing still. Set into a spear-shaft or a shoulder-plate it adds a quarter to whatever you were already committed to, and it adds it at the far end of the movement, once you have run out of ways to change your mind. Setters keep it out of knives, a knife being a stopping weapon and this being no sort of stopping stone. People who wear one arrive at the far side of things they had meant to go around.

lore.t: The war
the horse
comes out of is in no book, and
Bettany

has spent a whole circuit of fires establishing that it is in nobody's mouth either. What she has instead is ninety-two gold on a bench: grey plates, dead violet in the seams, a pale star at the middle. A stone is one fact pressed down until it is nearly a mineral, and the fact in this one is not running, and is not fear, and is not carrying a man. It is a shape. The middle of a row, at a flat gallop, without checking. Which means there were rows, and somebody stood men in them, and worked an animal at them morning after morning until that was the last thing left in it.

lore: So it is a document, the shortest she owns, and the only source in the Chronicle she can verify by picking it up. What buyers pay for is the second half of the effect, the part where whatever you hit goes backwards. None of that is the animal's. That is what a line looks like from the front.

heavy_iron_links.description: Three pitted iron links, worn smooth where a harness rubbed. The Nightmule that wore it is still out there.

lore.t: There is a carter at the east crossing who pays nine gold a set for these and is not melting them. He is rebuilding the rig. He has the breeching, most of a collar, a bridle with one cheekpiece, a pad — all of it picked up off the ground behind
the mule that still keeps its route

— and he is short two trace chains and a hame strap. Ask what he means to do with a finished harness and he will tell you flatly: put it on. Not to stop the animal. It has never minded being touched, and it has never once stopped. He wants to load it, and walk at its head, and be the voice up front, since the voice it halts for is not coming.
Wendell
has offered to name him the stops on the old road. He says he will take that when the rig is done.

heavy_long_bone.description: One heavy leg bone, clean at both ends. Gravecharger is missing several and has not noticed.
lore: Seven gold, and the glue you boil out of it is worth more than the bone, which is the first economics anybody in this trade learns and about the only lesson that sticks. Two days at a rolling simmer, skim, reduce, cool it to a slab: the size that holds a haft to a head and a bow to itself.

lore.t: Osric

buys them by the sack and complains about the smell in the same words every time, which the whole smithy can now say along with him. He has costed it twice and found both times he would do better buying glue ready-made. He boils bones anyway, on the grounds that a smith who buys everything he uses is a shopkeeper. Ask what he does with the difference and he changes the subject, because he is putting it by in
gold
, and does not know what for, and has not for two years.

hollow_black_soulstone.description: Cracked all the way through, with nothing in the cracks. What reached the bottom of this one was never its own.

lore.t: A soulstone is the bottom of a creature: one fact, one appetite, pressed to mineral. This one comes out of
Grinmask

cracked all the way through, and there is nothing in the cracks. Not damage — they all come out like that. The trade's working explanation is short and unpleasant: that shape was emptied long before anyone broke it, so what settled to the bottom of it was never the creature's own. It was the visitor's.
By that reading, everyone who carries one is carrying a fragment of
the thing under the mountain
. Several people have pointed this out. Nobody has stopped. The exception is
Hearn
, who has been nearer the source than anyone: he sold his the same evening it was paid to him, under its price, to a buyer he did not look at.

hooked_bat_wing.description: Leathery brown membrane on finger-bones, with a claw at the crown. Whatever flies on these keeps to its cave.

lore.t: Look at the hook, not the wing. The inner curve is polished — not scuffed, polished, the way a stair rail goes under sixty years of the same hand — which means the animal hangs, and hangs in one place, often enough to wear horn smooth against rock. Somewhere there is a ceiling with a groove worn into it. A cracker worked all that out over a winter, was extremely pleased with himself, and carried the wing east to put it to
Hearn

, who has been inside the only cave anyone means when they say the cave. Hearn turned it over twice, looked at the polish rather than the claw, said not that one, and handed it back. Twenty-two gold, and the wing is the cheap half of what you are buying. The rest is a room nobody has found.

iridescent_nacre_shard.description: Turn this flake of shell and it shifts green to violet. The dune gave it up; whatever grew it is long fossil.

lore.t: The broken edge is not one thing. It is about four hundred things, stacked: layer on layer on layer, each one a season of some flat, patient animal adding a little more house. That is all the colour is. Not a pigment — a count. Green going to violet is what four hundred years of doing the same small job, once a year, does to daylight coming through it. The water it worked in has been gone from that country since before anyone woke there. The sand turned its back plate up in a clean hollow behind a
delver
, and somebody dropped it in a bag with eleven other flakes and walked on, and it is worth sixty gold. The patient are not paid at a better rate than anyone else.

iridescent_prism_stone.description: A mosaic that changes colour every time you look away, off a Prismclaw. It lies a hand's width from where it looks.

lore.t: Appraisers pick this one up with their eyes shut, and there is no trick to it beyond knowing there is one. Light comes off the mosaic bent, so the stone is never quite where the cloth says it is, and a confident hand closes on nothing. Dealers' children learn it as a party piece years before they learn prices. The offset is always to the same side, which is the whole of the item: carry one a day and you are reaching a finger's width off for your own cup without having decided to. In a fight the good hit arrives, and then arrives again, half as hard, beside itself. Hunters in
that country
are taught before anything else to aim beside what they can see.

lore: Tap one and it gives a single high note, the same note off every stone of the kind, and any smith will tell you what that note means in a piece of steel: a flaw running the whole way through, an edge that is going to let go, and the only question left is which stroke. Nothing of the sort has ever happened. They do not chip and they do not part. It is a lie the stone has apparently always told, and it is also the fastest way to sort one from the leavings — out in the crystal country there are smooth boulders with snapped points scattered round the base, and people gather them up and sell them along the road as chips of the real thing, four gold, most of them honestly enough. Tapped, the points say nothing at all. They came off an animal trying to rub off something that was itself.

ivory_hooked_talon.description: Cream-white and curved to a needle point, the socket left ragged. Glowbones and Frostwraiths grow them in sets.
lore: Bore out the ragged end, bind it into a haft, and you have the best awl in the country: a point that goes through four thicknesses of hide and does not blunt, ever, however much of it you do. Every sail-mender, harness-maker and tent-patcher on the northern rounds is sewing with one. They cost more than the tools they replace, and the people who use them do not haggle.

lore.t: Where they come from is the part the trade steps around. There is a boy who walks the low edge of the high snow, picking them out of the drift where a
Frostwraith

has been working, and he brings down a dozen at a time. He will not say how far up he goes. The answer is plain enough to anyone who has been. No one at that fire asks him, and several of them are sewing while they do not ask.

jade_temple_amulet.description: A green disc with a pale gem set dead centre. Temple work, and Runemane still guards a heap of it.

lore.t: Eighty gold, and it moves faster than anything else off that field, for the plainest reason in the trade: it is the only piece of the place a person can wear.
The cogs
are a curiosity.
The little folded figures
unsettle people. This is a green disc with a stone in the middle, it hangs well, it does not chip, and you can put it on.

lore: So a lot of them are on. Count round any decent fire on the eastern road and you will find two or three, and their owners will tell you, correctly, that it is temple work, and that is the end of what any of them knows. Whatever the hall was for, whatever was said in it, whatever a person was undertaking while wearing one of these — that went with the walls. The disc came through. The trade priced it and passed it along, and there is not one person left who could tell the wearers whether they are allowed to.

large_white_pearl.description: One flawless sphere, off-white with a lilac sheen. Nobody will say which water it was brought up out of.
lore: Gold buys goods. A pearl is what you put on the table when the thing you want is not for sale, and at a hundred and ten it is well clear of the price of anything a person actually needs.

lore.t: A man set one down in front of
Bettany
and asked her to leave a name out of
the Chronicle

. Not his own. She did not take it and she did not argue with him. She wrote the offer down instead — the date, the sphere, the lilac in it, what it would have fetched, and the fact that a man had believed the book was the sort of thing that could be bought, which she noted was the more interesting half of the evening. She left his name out. That part he did get.

lava_vein_stone.description: Black stone flooded with slow orange veins, quenched out of a Slagfang. Still too warm to pocket.
lore: You cannot pocket one. Every new collector tries it once and buys a tin the same afternoon, and every bag that has worked the burnt country has a scorch inside where somebody learned. It does not cool. Held bare it sits at the limit of what a hand will agree to, and the trade's word for that is the honest one: quenched, not burning. Nothing runs out of it and nothing gets in.

It does the same for a fighter. Wounds shut as fast as they open; you do not bleed with one on you. A wolf that went into a caldera and came out with the seams standing open in its hide lost nothing through them either, and that flat fact is the whole of what reached the bottom.

lore.t: Every one of these ever brought in came down out of the east. Not most — every one, off a country
Solveig

has never walked and does not intend to. She has met nine of them at the other end of it, in the grass, when they are still only wet animals that cannot stand, and every one of them left her going the same way.

So she buys. Anyone coming down out of the burnt country with a stone gets the asking price without haggling, and inside the week she sells it on for exactly that, losing nothing, gaining nothing. What she keeps is the few days between: a warm thing in a cloth by her fire that has been where they were going.
The wolf
need not be one of hers. She knows that. She holds it anyway.

layered_fern_fronds.description: One frond still furled tight, layered like a fist, already going gold along the outer edge.

lore.t: Hearn

keeps one in a cup of water on a sill and turns the cup a quarter every morning. He came back from the mountain alone and will not give one word about the inside. He will talk about the fern to anybody, at length, given the smallest opening.

lore: Cut furled, it goes on. That is the trick and the whole price — an hour later it has opened on the stem and it is a leaf, quite pretty, worth nothing. His opened in the cup over nine days, one turn at a time. By the sixth people were putting their heads round the door to look. By the eighth there were too many of them in the room and someone had carried a chair up. Very little here gets bigger. Nobody says that out loud, and a fern in a cup says it for them, and every one of them went home fed.

lichen_crusted_rock.description: A fist of rock crusted in grey-green lichen. Cragback is made of these, and misses each one when it goes.

lore.t: The lichen is a clock. It wants forty still years to come in that thick, and a face that has just lost a stone is bare — so the pale patches on a
Cragback
are a robbery ledger, readable from the next ridge and dated by how far the green has crept back over them.

lore: Which is how the trade found out the thing it does not repeat at fires. A well-robbed one is slower. Take enough off a hillside and the hillside labours, so the crews go back to the animals they have already opened, because those are the easy ones, and they keep going back, and the bare faces spread. A crusted fist of rock fetches eight. A day's walk out and a day's walk back, for eight.

lichen_green_soulstone.description: Mottled olive crust over smooth grey, dark in the seams. A Mirewart's last piece; small hurts close as you walk.
lore: The commonest stone there is: dealers do not count them, they weigh them, and a bagful has bought a first winter's boots for a great many people who came to the fires with nothing else to sell. The trade calls it a walking stone — it works between places and never during. Carry one across a long day and there is no moment you feel it; at the fire, the day's small hurts have closed without ceremony.

lore.t: The part worth more thought is who keeps them. A great many people are still carrying the first one they ever took, years past affording better, and
Bettany
has been collecting their reasons for
the Chronicle

: it is lucky, it is paid for, it sits right in a pocket. She notes that not one reason quite holds, and that every keeper can still say exactly where the water was and how the light sat on it. The first thing a frightened newcomer breaks in this country is very often
a slow green weight
that did not run, and what they carry up from the mud is this. Kept, she has written, the way an apology is kept by people who would rather carry it than say it.

linen_thread_spool.description: Half a spool of plain linen thread. Something stitched the Palehusk together, and it was not a tailor.

lore.t: Dealers will tell you what the sewing on
the walking things

was for. They are guessing. The spool is the interesting part: every one that has ever come in off the black rock is half used, and ask ten people who have handled one to describe it and you get the same half, down to the tail of thread hanging loose at the side.

lore: A woman at a fire on the north road took hers in payment two winters ago and has mended out of it since — eleven coats, a tent wall, a boot she had no business saving. It is exactly as full as the day she got it. She stopped mentioning that at about the fourth coat, because of how people's faces went. She has not stopped sewing, and she would like it on record, if anybody is keeping one, that she got eleven coats out of a thing the rest of them were afraid to touch.

loose_beast_teeth.description: Molars, curved fangs and small incisors, no two from the same jaw. Palemaws and Emberjaws shed them constantly.
lore: Eight gold the mixed lot, and the mixing is the trade's teaching tool. Somebody tips a bag out on a cloth at a fire, the new ones go round the ring naming each tooth to its animal, whoever gets one wrong stands the next drink. It is a good evening. Everybody has had it.

lore.t: There is a hard edge under the game and the old hands put it there deliberately. Two teeth in every bag are dog. One is off a
Rotjaw
, which will stand at the head of a farm track for a hundred years and never come at you. The other is off a
Blightcur

, which will lie down twenty paces off and not come at you either. A cracker who cannot tell those two apart on a cloth, in good light, with all the time in the world, will one day sit down and rest in the wrong company.

loose_vertebrae.description: Three vertebrae still loosely strung together. Gravecharger sheds them and does not slow down.

lore.t: Boil the gristle off, run a cord through the holes, and a spine becomes the cheapest counter anybody ever made: one bone pushed down the string for each night kept.
Jehanne

has used the same one since she took up the rite — a short string, nine bones, because nine was the length of the rota she was handed and it has never been revised down for her. She pushes one along after the candles are out. When the ninth goes she runs them all back to the top and starts again, and she has done that more times than she has a number for, on a rota that has not had nine keepers on it in a very long time. Ten gold buys you the string. What you count on it afterwards is your own business.

matte_black_shadow_stone.description: Matte black, softly faceted, handing back no light at all. In a full pouch you find this one by touch, not by eye.

lore.t: Stones are sorted on a dark cloth by lamplight, and every one says something on the way down — a coin of light, a stripe. This one lands and there is only cloth where it landed. Old hands still count the row twice before tying the bag. The fix is
Sigrun
's: any pouch that leaves her bench with one of these inside has a bright thread sewn to it, no charge, no comment. You check the thread.

Set in a blade it is the not-being-seen, finished and portable. Fights end, and the ending does not particularly include you: the shape goes down looking at somebody else. Off a creature that spent its whole loud life
charging head-first
, that is the stone's one correction — the charge was the noise. The bottom fact was never being looked at.

lore: Sigrun also keeps one loose in her apron, unset. A smithy is a place where people stand about and watch your hands, and on the days when the work on the bench is a cracking, she would rather the watching slid off.

matted_black_pelt.description: Coarse black fur clumped and matted, with stray quills caught in it. Something out there is patchy now.

lore.t: Nineteen gold. It was nineteen ten years ago and it is nineteen today, and
gold

is supposed to be the only thing in this country that holds a number like that. You cannot card the fur or tan it, and the quills caught through it come off something small that had no business bedding down that close to something that size — which is also why it cannot be faked. A dealer out west set out to break the price and brought forty in at once. He was paid nineteen gold, forty times over, by a factor who counted them out, asked nothing and wrote no name in the book. He has not tried it again, and he has stopped joking about who is at the far end of that chain.

mint_serpent_stone.description: Mint-green with a serpent coiled across it, left by a Blightcur. Whatever it carries, it survives.

lore.t: Sellers of this one demonstrate before they name a price. The cloth comes off, the stone goes into a bare palm — mint-green, cool, a serpent coiled across the face of it in low relief — and it stays there as long as the customer cares to stand and watch, because a whole class of buyer will not touch one otherwise. This is the useful thing the stone says that
the animal

never will. Sit inside twenty paces of that dog and it costs you something you do not get back. Carry its last hard piece all winter and it costs you nothing, ever, and no handler has yet taken so much as a foul week off one. The sickness was cargo. What reached the bottom was the carrying — which is why a blade with one set in it leaves a wound that goes on working long after the blade has gone elsewhere.
Wendell

owns one, and people find that funny for about as long as it takes him to explain it. He is old and does not walk far, so he is on the short list of people a fire has to be moved for when that line comes round; it has happened to him twice. The young walker who carried his things the second time came back a season later and put the stone on his sill without much of a speech. Wendell could sell it for two winters of firewood. He would rather look at it, because it is the only proof anyone has brought him that one of those rounds ended.

mint_slime_globule.description: Mint-green, translucent, and lit by a pale core. Every pond blob in the valley leaves one behind, wobbling.

lore.t: A broken
pond-dweller

leaves the light behind in it, and that light is no use at all for seeing by and perfect for being seen. Set one on a stone at dusk and it is still findable at midnight and gone by the next night, so the valley walkers buy them ten at a time and mark their way in at the junctions.

lore: One at a junction means a walker went that way. Two means come and get me. That is the entire code and it has not changed in the working memory of anyone using it. There is a man on the pond circuit who has marked his route in and out for eleven years and has never once set the second, and the fire he walks back to keeps a standing agreement about the night he does: the pot comes off, and everybody goes.

mire_stained_claw.description: A green-grey claw with fen mud dried in the cracks. Mireglare keeps four sets and uses them all.

lore.t: Never buy a clean one. Fen mud sets into the cracks like grout and it is half the goods: it tells you which bank, which season, and whether the claw has been out of the water as long as the seller says it has. People working
Mireglare

country grade the mud before they so much as look at the point — which is exactly why the fen road has a small trade in mud. There is a man on it who sells the stuff by the thumbful, correct colour, correct bank, and everybody knows, and the grading goes on regardless, because the alternative is saying out loud that the only thing anyone can truly check about a piece of junk is what colour it is.

molten_gold_vein_stone.description: Rough brown rock seamed with raw gold, grazed loose by an Amethyrn. Coin comes easier to whoever carries it.
lore: It does not find gold. Any honest seller says that first and the price second and has no third thing to say. What it does is make you sure. Carry one and you will be certain about the next foot of rock, or about which of two roads has the paying end, in the flat unarguable way you are certain of your own hand — and you will be right often enough that two hundred and sixty gold starts to look like a bargain.

lore.t: Often enough is not always, and the men carrying them cannot tell those two apart from the inside. A digger who has been right four times running will tell you he read the ground. He cannot say whether he found the seam or the stone walked him onto it, and by the fifth time it has stopped occurring to him to wonder.
The trade's own line
is that a soulstone does not make you stronger, it makes you harder to argue with. This is the one where that stops being a compliment.
The stone itself is rough brown rock with raw gold standing up in the seams of it, warm, heavy, and workable by no one, so that
the one substance here that never drifts

sits inside the one substance here that cannot be forgotten. Scholars enjoy that a great deal. The diggers have the better observation and it is shorter: certainty is not knowledge, it is only what knowledge feels like from the inside.
Amethyrn
is never wrong about a hill. It is the size of a cart, and it is out east walking around made of the stuff.

molten_lava_soulstone.description: Blackened shell webbed with live lava, cut out of a Magmane. A weapon takes its fire and leaves things burning.

lore.t: The standing argument about
the lion

is whether any of the heat is its own. It is Made, so nothing in it ever lived anywhere else: remembering that gathered at a volcano's throat, thickened, and stood up. And everything on that ground is hot, the boulders included. Stand close and you have stood near a hot animal on hot rock, with nothing in it you can separate.

lore: The stone settles that. A blackened shell webbed with live lava, brightest where the webs meet; two hundred and eighty-five gold; and still exactly that hot at the bottom of a pack four hundred miles west, in a wet country, in winter, with the mountain nowhere in it. The heat came away when the stone did.

Off an edge it goes in and stays in: what you struck is still burning while you decide what to do next. That follows from the animal. The fire is shut under the glass and opens only once it has decided about you, and it does not decide twice.

lore.t: Sigrun

charges for the iron rather than the setting — a housing that touches a web has to be forged around the stone in place, with the stone in the fire throughout and indifferent to it. She has done four. Over each one she says the same sentence to whoever is paying, in the flat voice she keeps for people who want a thing and would rather not know about it: this will still be doing that when you have stopped.

moss_green_slime.description: A green dome flecked with moss, still cool. The forest blobs leave one behind every time they lose.

lore.t: Cool for hours, and it will not take heat off a hand, which is the only property in this whole part of the trade that a person can actually use.
Jehanne

keeps a crock of them by her fire and puts one on a burn, a barked knuckle, a blister off a bad boot, the way somebody's grandmother did it. Whether any of that is needed here is a question she has stopped raising, on the same reasoning as everything else she still does: the hand hurts, the hand goes cool, the person sits down and stays a while. Seven gold the crock. The wood restocks it every time it loses.

mossy_driftwood_bundle.description: Grey, water-worn branches still furred with moss. Break a Stumpling and this is most of what is left.

lore.t: The dealers sort by the ends. Water breaks a branch ragged; a blade does not. A bundle with clean ends came off a
Stumpling

that was walking that morning, and it is the same wood, and it burns the same, and it goes for less anyway — six gold, against eight for the honest sort, and it is the cheapest heat there is either way.

lore: One shore fire took a load of the cut sort in a wet season and it burned green for the better part of an hour. Nobody said anything about it. The talk went thin and then stopped, and people found reasons to turn in early, and in the morning the fire was banked and swept and somebody had been out to the woodpile in the dark and sorted the whole of it into two heaps.

mossy_granite_stone.description: Grey granite gone green with moss, off a Cragback. It weighs what a hillside weighs, in the hand.

lore.t: You do not go hunting a
Cragback

. You buy a sighting, and a sighting comes from somebody who has stood in one doorway at one hour of the evening for eighty years and can tell you the line of the hill is not the line of the hill. Crews pay for that, by the sighting, in gold, and it is the only work in the country whose entire qualification is having looked at the same thing your whole life without once getting bored of it.

lore: What comes out is grey, green in the seams, brown-crusted along one flank, and it weighs what it has no business weighing; handlers take it in two hands without deciding to. Set into armour it makes you hard to get through, which is what the sheet says and not what anybody buys it for. They buy the other half: bridge-holders, the two or three who still stand at the gorge crossings, anyone whose work is being exactly where they were put while something large arrives.

At the bottom of a made thing is whatever made it, and this one was made by a hundred valleys' worth of people agreeing about a hill — the same dark line against the same evening, generation on generation, not one of them ever giving an inch on it. That is the fact in your fist, and it has nothing to do with strength. It is about not being argued out of a position. Two hundred and forty-five gold, and the old man who sold the sighting is back in his doorway at the same hour, learning the new line, because a hill that has moved once is a hill you no longer know.

mossy_green_egg.description: Dark green plates shut around a yellow-green star, and the moss on them is still growing. It cuts and it mends.
lore: The only piece that is still doing something. Set one on a shelf and leave it a year and the moss has got further — a plate's width up the shaded side, on a stone fed nothing and watered by nothing. People who handle stones by the sackful stopped finding that remarkable long ago, and still keep this one where they can see it.

The trade's one argument is where to put it, because the stone does not care. Growth goes into whatever it is set against: turned outward on an edge it opens a shape faster than the shape can close, worn against the ribs it closes the wearer while they are still being opened. Same work. It is not doing two things.

lore.t: Hearn

wears his sewn into the lining, ribs side, and has kept it there since before the mountain. His ruling on the argument is the longest sentence most people have got out of him: a thing that cannot tell cutting from mending, you keep on your own side of the fight. He paid
a Mosscairn's
fist for it, and calls the price fair, which from Hearn is a review.

mossy_root_stone.description: Dull olive under a dark web of root, plain enough to lose in the grass. Your cuts close over and your blows come up green.
lore: Stones are weighed by hand before they are weighed by scale, and the hand is hunting appetite: a piece off something that burned sits in the palm with a want that comes through a glove. This one sits there like a stone — matte olive, no shine, easy to lose in grass — and the trade priced it accordingly for years. Wrongly. The flattest ones are not empty; their want is pointed at something other than you.

lore.t: Carry one and the pointing shows: by evening the small hurts have closed unnoticed and the day's work has come apart readier than the edge explains. Everything else off a
Nightmule

is about a person who is not there. The stone alone is about the animal, and there is no owner in it at any depth — whoever walked at the front never reached the bottom. What reached the bottom was the going on, unloaded, in a straight line. That is the part in your pocket.

olive_buried_gold_stone.description: Olive-grey and speckled, with a fleck of gold buried dead centre that nobody has got out. Off a Dunedelver.

lore.t: Hold it up and the gold is right there — a few grains of it, a finger's depth inside speckled olive rock with no seam and no crack to reach it by. Every owner tries once.
Gold
is the one substance here that does not drift, remembered identically by everyone who ever handled any, and there is not one account anywhere of a grain of it coming out of one of these.
Osric

tried properly, being a smith and being new enough to take a thing like this for a problem rather than a fact. He gave it a full working day. The stone came up to heat and stayed a stone, the gold in the middle of it stayed precisely where it was, and at the end he had a warm stone and a shop full of people who had come round to watch. It is still on his bench. He says it holds paper down.

What it does in the field is what the animal does. Sand is the one ground in this country that keeps nothing: put a thing under a dune and the dune hands it back, upright and clean, a season later. The stone works the same way on a fight — you take what there is, you finish, you turn away, and now and then the ground gives up one more piece behind you off a thing you were done with. There is no explaining why it should.
The delver
is not looking for anything either.

one_eyed_steel_mask.description: Grim steel with cheek guards and a third eye cut above the slits. Somebody hammered it, and that is the comfort.

lore.t: A bag coming back off the ground where
Grinmask

works can have two masks in it, and telling them apart takes no expertise at all. This one is hammer work. The inside is a mess of tool marks, the strap boss has been replaced by a hand that could not match the original rivet, and the third eye above the brow was cut freehand and sits a hair off the centre line, by a man who noticed, and shrugged, and sold it anyway. It is grim on purpose. Grim was what the customer wanted.

lore: The other kind has no marks in it anywhere, and the trade does not price that kind, and does not carry it at the top of the bag.

Ninety-five gold, and there are crackers who wear this one working the same ground it came off. Ask them why and they will tell you about the cheek guards. The cheek guards are a quarter-inch of soft steel and would not stop a dog.

opal_bubble_stone.description: An opal shell of soap-bubble colours. Beautiful, valuable, and belonging to nothing anyone has met.

lore.t: Two hundred and sixty-five gold on a good day, and the honest sellers will tell you the number is invented. A price in this trade is a story about a creature: how hard it is to find, how hard it is to break the shape, how many crackers walked home. Take the creature out and the floor goes with it.
Gold

is the one substance in the country that never drifts, which is precisely why the drift shows here — the same stone has changed hands at forty and at four hundred inside one season, and both sellers went home pleased.

lore: It earns some of that. An opal shell in soap-bubble colours, cells of pink and cyan and gold shut in by fine dark seams, the whole surface moving as your hand turns without one of those colours actually being in it. Worn, the first blow of a fight glances off, and after that you are simply hard to lay a hand on.

lore.t: Bettany

keeps a page for it that is nothing but a column of dates. Fourteen sales she can confirm across eleven years, and every one goes back exactly one hand and stops — a buyer who had it from a seller who had it from a man he can describe and cannot name. She gave up for a while, because every seller answers and every answer is true. Then she took it up again. The missing creature does not trouble her much; the rule everyone learns first says there is one, and she can be patient. What troubles her is the supply. They arrive in ones, out of different directions, and they keep arriving.

opal_moon_stone.description: Pale opal that holds a crescent whichever way you turn it. Moonpelt's own, and the moon wants it back.
lore: Every other stone is a fact and works in a tin. This one wants a condition. Indoors it is a pretty object — milky, lilac and mint and cyan moving under the surface, a crescent standing in the seams that stays put however you turn your wrist. Out under open sky at night it shuts a wound while you are still deciding whether to sit down, and nothing gets a clean hand on you.

Which is why the tellers dislike it, and they are not wrong to. The whole of the Keeping is people sitting still in one place with a fire and each other; a stone that pays a man to be out on a road under the moon instead is, put politely, an argument against the rota. Sellers put it the other way round — the fires are far apart now and somebody has to walk between them — and both sides have had their piece ready for years and neither has moved an inch.

lore.t: Wendell

walks at night and will not have one in the house. He is pleasant about it and does not lecture, and anyone who has sat with him works out why unaided: every one of these was somebody's payment for breaking a
Moonpelt

, and one of those holds thirty paces behind him over broken ground and comes no nearer than the edge of the light. Watch the animal all night and you can still tell yourself the frost under those paws is the light playing tricks. Carry the stone one night and the argument closes. The not-touching was the last hard thing in there. It is in your pocket, and it is working on you.

opal_shell_flake.description: A curved flake of shell that runs green to gold as you turn it. The dune keeps giving these up.
lore: Somebody on the dune circuit worked out that a flake on a wire turns in the wind, and a turning flake throws green, then gold, then nothing, over and over, further into the dark than firelight carries. So the dune fires wear collars of them now: two dozen strung along a wire between the stones, flashing all night, so that a person out there with no idea where they are has something to walk at.

lore.t: The wire outlasts the keeper.
Gunnar

has come in on four of them and found cold stones and no one, and he has left every wire hanging. His reasoning is short and he does not offer it twice: the flashing still fetches a stranger to a windbreak, a ring of stones and somewhere out of the sand, and that is not nothing, and it is a great deal more than the dark straight on.

orange_lightning_stone.description: Orange stone forked with white light. It hums in sunlight, and no creature yet has answered for it.
lore: The hum is not audible across a room and never has been. It is in the hand, and only in sun: carry one into shade and it stops inside a breath, take it out and it is back before your fingers close. Two hundred and fifty gold, orange plates forked through with white. In a weapon it burns, and it burns worst at whatever has been longest out of the light.

A man on the western roads has carried one for forty years. He does not fight with it and has never had it set. The pocket has been re-sewn nine times and the stone is exactly as it was the day he was paid it — a stone cannot be forgotten, so it cannot wear, so it outlasts the patience of the man carrying it by a margin that does not bear working out. He takes work that moves. A man who stays where he is meets what comes past him; a man who keeps going meets more.

lore.t: What he is waiting for is whatever this came out of, and he has a description ready and no evidence for any of it: something that stands out in the open at the top of the day, something that hums. He has never heard it anywhere but in his own hand. Asked what he means to do if it is ever in front of him, he does not say break it. He says he will do it
the courtesy
— sit down a little way off, ask its name and one true thing. He knows how that sounds. He has known for forty years and has not changed the answer.

pair_of_molars.description: Two grinders with forked roots, one big enough for a Diretusk. Both chewed harder things than grass.

lore.t: Nine gold, and worth it only to the one man on that road who can read them. Hand him a molar and he will give you the animal and the age to the season: a
Nightmule
's at eleven years, a
Diretusk

's at more than he has numbers for, a brute's not at all, because a brute grinds against rock and its teeth lie about the years. He was a horseman. He is not a great deal else now. People bring him teeth for the trick and he does the trick, and they pay him in company, which is the going rate. What he cannot do is name the last horse he owned. He has been asked twice, kindly, by two different people, each of whom decided afterwards not to ask again.

paired_black_claws.description: A matched pair of glossy black hooks, sharp as the day they grew. Duskfang and its cousins do not give them up.

lore.t: Worn on a thong, a matched pair says one thing and says it loudly: I have stood in front of a
Duskfang
and I am here to be asked about it.

lore: A woman on the black-wood rounds wore hers for two years before she had earned them. She bought them, eight over the going rate, from a man who knew precisely what she was buying and handed them across without a word about it. She has since done the thing twice, properly, with people watching, which by any reckoning settles the account. She still will not take them off. The man is still on that road and still nods to her at the crossing, and in all the years since neither of them has said one syllable about it, and she has worked out by now that the nod is the part she cannot give up.

pale_armoured_beetle.description: Palm-sized and bone-pale, its plated back mottled tan, six legs tucked under. The valley's small fry all carry one.

lore.t: Twelve gold is a lot for a common thing, and the reason is that they are a nuisance to reach: they sit deep, and you have to break a
Sprigling

open properly to get one out. Children manage it faster than grown men and for less. So a pale beetle in a child's pocket is a confession — it says which end of the valley, on which afternoon, against what they were told. Most of that road has agreed not to notice. Twelve gold is twelve gold, and the sacks pay for boots.

pale_bat_wing.description: Tan membrane on pale finger bones, torn free mid-flight. The gaunt things that haunt the drifts fly on these.

lore.t: Eleven hundred and six. A woman on the north road has walked the same two miles of drift at every thaw for thirty years, picking pale wings out of the melt, and that is her count. They come down whole and they come down alone — no other bone, no fur, no teeth, nothing else of whatever was carrying them, not once in eleven hundred. She sells enough to keep herself in boots and no more. Every autumn she sends the year's figure to
the Chronicle
with no letter attached, because there is nothing to say about it yet. What she wants is to be there in the year the number stops.

pale_blue_crystal_cluster.description: Ice-blue spires on a common base, cold indoors and out. Rimeshard grows this in its rock and swings the rest.
lore: The test is your own neck. Hold a spire under the jaw for a slow count of twenty.
