True frost quartz does not come up to meet you — it stays precisely as cold as it was, and afterwards the skin aches. Dyed quartz warms by about eight. An honest seller offers you the count before you ask for it.

lore.t: The forgers got around this in the obvious way. They sell in hard weather, when everything in the world is cold and the count proves nothing, and they sell to people three weeks out of
the grass
, who do not yet know that anything here is bought or sold, and who will hand over a coin they carried through an entire life for a stone that is going to disappoint them in April.

pale_blue_hailstones.description: Blue-white pebbles, a good dozen, that will not melt in the palm. Whatever a Frostling is packed from, this is it.
lore: They are sold by the dozen because the game takes twelve. Every era that arrives here brought its own version — knucklebones, jacks, five-stones — and rime pebbles are what the game settled on in the cold country, being the one counter that will not warm, wear, or roll off true.

lore.t: There is a patch on the north side of the meadow with eleven of them still in the grass, in a rough ring, where a throw was interrupted a long time ago.
Solveig
cuts around it. Asked why she does not just gather them up, she says she will. The twelfth is in her apron pocket and has been for nine years.

pale_bone_soulstone.description: Chalk-cream, crazed edge to edge with fine dark fissures, and not one of them gives. In armour it refuses to come apart.
lore: Hand one to somebody new and watch the thumb. The whole surface is crazed, fine dark fissures dividing the chalk-cream into panels like a flat of dried mud, and every pair of hands new to it presses, gently, to find out how near the thing is to coming apart. It does not give. The trade keeps a short demonstration for buyers who will not take that on trust, involving a bench and the flat of a hammer, and the stone wins.

lore.t: It stays cheap all the same, and the reason is honest: there is nothing to feel. In armour it pays out at the one moment you would otherwise not be getting up, and that is a hard thing to sell to anyone who has never been on the ground.
Solveig

keeps the fire the broken re-form beside, and has sat with what comes back — minus a little of what it was thinking — often enough to have a settled opinion. She gives every new bag-carrier heading out the same advice: past the bright stones, buy the dull one. The ones who laugh at the price have not been on the ground either. She says it pleasantly, once, and does not argue. Her fire will make the case for her some night, whichever stone they chose.

pale_curved_horn.description: A pale horn with one clean curve, snapped at the base. Gravecharger wears a pair and notices neither.
lore: Split it, boil it soft, press it flat and it goes translucent: four panes to a horn, thin enough to see a flame through and tough enough to laugh at wind. That is the horner's whole trade, and the reason a fire on an open fell stays lit in weather. A pane costs less than a candle and outlives forty of them.

lore.t: The joke among horners is that the finest stock in the country grows on
Gravecharger

, and getting any is a matter of standing in the right place at a very wrong moment. In fact they walk its lines, which run straight and are close to the last straight thing out that way, and pick up what it sheds and does not miss. Every lantern on the old eastern circuit was glazed like this, back when there was a circuit. The horners are still cutting panes, and could not tell you now who buys them.

pale_green_core_stone.description: Pale green plates around a white core, warm as a greenhouse. Nobody has found what grows them.

lore.t: Solveig
keeps hers in the apron, left pocket, and has done for longer than most of the people on that meadow have been
awake

. What is broken re-forms beside the nearest tended fire, and hers is the nearest tended fire for a long way in three directions, so she has had a great deal of practice at the hour afterwards — somebody sitting in the grass with their hands going, short a little of whatever they had been thinking about. She puts the stone into those hands and holds them shut around it until they can manage a cup. Pale green plates around a white middle, warm the way a glasshouse is warm. It does the rest.

lore: Dealers have explained to her, more than once, what she is carrying. That the plates and the white core match nothing anyone has ever broken open. That by every rule of the trade a stone with no shape behind it should not exist. That a collector in the south would pay well for it and ask her nothing. She says that is nice, and thanks them, and goes back to the fire.

Pressed on why she is not curious, she gives the same answer she gives to everything, which is the oldest courtesy there is: you ask a newly woken soul their name and one true thing, and you do not ask where they came from, because for most of them the answer is a hole and the asking widens it. She has never seen why a stone should be handled worse than a person. Seventy-eight gold, forty years, an apron pocket. Her hands are bad in the cold, and it is good for that too.

pale_grey_brain.description: Whole, pink and unpleasantly warm. Palehusk carries spares, which explains a great deal about Palehusk.

lore.t: Thirty-five gold is most of a week, and it comes out of the head, and the head is the last thing you do. There is a woman on the black-rock circuit who brings in four or five a season and is entirely plain about it: feet first, work upward, bag open on the stone and not in your lap. She says releasing at the counter and
the other word

at the fire, and means both. Warm is not the same as occupied, she says. Holding that difference is the whole of the job, and anybody who cannot hold it should go and do something else, with her blessing, today.
She keeps one rule that has nothing to do with the work. When it is
one of the person-shaped ones
, she closes the hand first — folds the open fingers over, before she starts on anything else. It does nothing for the shape. It is not for the shape.

pale_grey_eyeball.description: A grey eye with the light gone out of it. Palehusk collects them, which is not a comforting thought.

lore.t: A sorter at the fen counter set one aside out of a new bag and asked the plain question: where on the animal was it. The cracker could not say. Neither could the next one asked, nor anyone on that road since. They are picked out of the grass afterwards, at the edge of the pressed circle, loose, never attached to the thing that came down. And what
that one
leaves is a mask, and the mask has no eyes in it and never had; the inward side is smooth.

lore: So the trade did what the trade does. Named it Pale Eye, priced it at twenty-six, agreed the price, stopped asking. Ask at a stall today and you will be told they come off Grinmask, which is where they come from and not where they were.

pale_hooked_claw.description: A cream claw hooked like a reaping tool, ragged at the socket. Bergclaw grows ten and uses all of them.

lore.t: North-rounds buyers price these by where they were picked up, which is not how anything else in the trade is priced. Off open ground, twenty-four gold. Found inside a fire's ring of stones, whatever the buyer can be talked into — and there is no agreed figure, because there has never yet been an instance. That is
Bergclaw

in one price: it comes for the warmth, sits out past the edge of the light the whole night, and leaves a claw in the sand for whoever slept badly. Keepers do not sell those. They carry them about in a pocket for a season or two, and that pocket is how the trade knows which fires had a visitor last winter.

pale_mist_swirl_stone.description: Pale grey and full of slow swirls, all a Nightmare leaves. Hold it and you will not recall your dreams.
lore: Every dealer of any standing keeps a book, and every book says the same thing about this one: it comes back. Never for a fault. It works perfectly for as long as you own it, which is the trouble. A fighter buys one, carries it a season, sleeps beautifully, and one morning sets it on the counter and takes two thirds of what they paid without arguing the price. Asked what is wrong with it, they cannot say. Most of them mention the weight.

lore.t: That book is harder evidence than anything written down about
the pale horse

itself. Watch it go by and you lose one night and do not miss it — nobody misses what they cannot remember having had. But one stone sold four times in six years out of the same shop, to four people who each thought better of it and none of whom could say why, is a measurement. It says the loss is real in the one place it cannot be felt, and it says so in a ledger, in a hand that was only keeping accounts.
There is one column that never turns round.
Hearn

buys them. Three so far, at the asking price, no haggling, and he has never sold one back; the dealers on that circuit know to hold one for him. He went into the mountain with a party and came out of it by himself, and he has made one statement about the inside in all the years since. He does not appear to need a second.

pale_moss_plate_stone.description: Pale green plates, cool and slightly damp. Some creature grows these; the valley has not shown it.
lore: Every stone in the country comes out of the grass warm and stays warm. Handlers grade by heft in the dark and the warmth is how the hand knows it has hold of a stone and not a pebble. This one is cool. Cool and faintly damp, pale green plates with a brighter seam at every crack, and it does not dry out — a dry shelf in a dry room through a dry month, and you pick it up and it is exactly as you left it. Forty gold. It turns up in junk lots between the teeth and the buckles.

lore.t: It is the stone people start with, and it is honestly good at what it is for: a whole season of moss and wet clay and slick root, and not once do you go down for footing. Press the graders and they will commit to one sentence, said flatly, on the way to something else — whatever reached the bottom of this spent its life keeping its feet in wet ground. That narrows the valley by about half. It narrows the list of things anyone has ever broken not at all, because this is not on that list. New hands ask. Old hands used to. Somewhere between the two the question aged out, the way questions do here when
the work
is steady and the answer costs money, and the stones go on arriving.

pale_moth_wing.description: Pale tan and ribbed brown, with a blue sheen at the base. Something big and soft-winged shed it in the dark.

lore.t: Handle one and a little of it comes away on your thumb, and what comes away does not go back. Most of the trade runs on that: an honest seller keeps them in paper, and the paper is the first thing to check, because a clean sheet means it has been touched twice and a floured one means it has been touched a hundred times. The bare ones are not fakes. They are the ones somebody carried in a pocket for a long while and finally sold.
Hearn
's is bare, and he did not sell it.

pale_ridged_horns.description: Four ivory horns splayed from one base, ridged like bark. Fiends and wraiths grow them for arguments they win.
lore: Twenty-four gold, and the honest bone in it is worth about two. What you are buying is the outline — four horns off one base, ridged like bark, and no other arrangement of plain bone in this country reads as hard as that across a room. The traders know precisely what they have. It goes high on the stack, three-quarters on, with the light coming up under it.

lore.t: It is the newly woken who buy them. A man three weeks into a country that is not the one he expected will not spend on a blanket and will spend on this, and hang it on a wall he does not own, in a room he will not keep, and it works — it is the first thing here that is his.
Solveig
has watched that happen a hundred times from the fire, and has never once talked anybody out of it.

pale_sand_stone.description: Sun-bleached plates cracked round a heart of gold, all a Dewling leaves. Blows land like a dropped weight, and dazzle.
lore: Cutlers keep the seams turned outward, for the flash: whatever takes the hit stands blinking at nothing for a second, and there is no light anywhere about to account for what it thinks it just saw. Bedded the wrong way, it is merely heavy.

The sorters grade them by how little colour is left. A sand-brown one came off ground somebody still walks. The bone-pale ones, seams gone nearly white, come off meadows a great many people remember and none of them visit any more, and fetch double. A strange way to price anything; the trade stopped finding it strange long ago.

lore.t: Bettany
came to the sorting sheds last autumn and copied ten years of grade-books into
the Chronicle
, price by price, and would not say what she wanted them for. She did not need to. Anyone can read a column that only climbs: every season the
Dewlings
come up a little paler, off a few more meadows going unwalked.

pale_silk_skein.description: Silvery cord wound tight and bound at the waist, cool to the touch. No hand in Nangijala spun this one.

lore.t: They arrive. Four or five a season at
Jehanne

's door, always overnight, always wound the same way and bound at the waist with the same two-turn knot, and in nine years she has not once caught whoever leaves them. No hand spun the cord — look close and the strands are laid rather than twisted — but a hand wound it into a skein and a hand tied that knot, and a knot is a habit, and a habit is a person. It is the strongest thread anybody here has, and twenty-six gold is cheap for it. Jehanne does not sell hers. She puts bread out on the nights she thinks one is coming, and the bread goes, and she has stopped telling people about it — the last time she did, three of them offered to sit up and watch with her, and she said no rather too fast.

pale_snowflake_stone.description: Near-white, with a six-armed star standing darker in the ice, out of a Bergclaw. Cold enough to ache through a glove.
lore: There is cold, and then there is this. It does not take the chill off a room and give it back; it is exactly as cold in a warm hand as in a snowbank, and after a while the ache comes up through the glove into the wrist and you set it down. Handlers keep them in wool under a wooden lid, grade them by eye, and do not linger over it.

lore.t: In a fight it does what frost does to rock. Cold does not shove a hard thing over — it gets inside and opens it. Shields come apart against this, not smashed but opened, and the next blow goes through a guard that was perfectly sound a moment before. The reading is the plainest in the trade: what went to the bottom of
Bergclaw
had learned that ice is not the soft part of a winter.
Solveig
has the other reading and has never offered it to a buyer.
The courtesy

is to sit with the newly woken and ask them their name and one true thing. She has met wakings she could not do that for — animals in the grass, no name to give, nothing to say — and she sits the hour out with them anyway and files it in her head under unfinished. A soulstone is one true thing, pressed down over centuries until it is very nearly mineral. This one is ninety-six gold and lives in a tin on a shelf. She has said what she thinks about that exactly once, and not to a buyer.

papery_hornet_nest.description: Tan paper in banded layers, one dark doorway low on the side. Prised out of a Stumpling's moss, and empty. Mostly.

lore.t: Boiled down it makes a passable paper, grey and tough, and that is the whole reason a nest is worth twenty-six gold while a handful of moss is worth nothing. The bands are worth more than the paper to the right buyer: one band a season, so a nest the size of a head has been building for eleven years, and the
Stumpling
carrying it has been standing in one spot that long. Put a stick in the doorway before it goes in your bag. Then wait. The man who taught everyone that rule is the man who did not.

pink_crystal_spikes.description: A spray of pink spires on a rough base. Pretty enough that people forget it came out of something that was walking.

lore.t: It takes no edge, holds no heat and does nothing whatever, which is why the trade calls it the coming-home stone. You have been a month on the road, you smell of
somebody else's leavings
, and you cannot make what you have been doing sound like a job — so you bring back the one thing in the bag that is only pretty.

lore: There is a woman on the west road with thirty-one of them along a windowsill and a husband still adding to them. She counted once, and worked out that she can name every month he was away and not one thing he did in it. She keeps them out anyway. She has thought it through and decided the sill is not a reproach; it is only the shape a marriage takes when one of you goes out and comes back.

pink_seam_granite_stone.description: Grey granite plates held by unbroken salmon-pink seams. In armour a crushing blow arrives as a shove, a fall as a bruise.
lore: It is not one piece, and that is the trade of it: grey granite plates held each to each by salmon-pink seams, so it holds the way a wall holds — by how it is joined. Struck along a seam it opens into two clean plates that both still work; struck across the grain, gravel. Reading the pink before the hammer falls is a living in itself.

lore.t: In armour it makes the ground feel closer: drops come off short, and what lands on you arrives without the part that was going to break something. The trade's sour rule holds here — stones off things that struck go into blades, and the stones that keep a person whole come off
a white creature
that never struck first in its existence, and spent the whole of it on one question: where to be standing when something heavy happens.
Hearn

wore one on the one organised walk anyone ever made on the cave. The others carried striking stones, and ribbed him the whole way east for armouring himself off a rabbit, and he let them. He came back alone, and unhollowed, and has never said whether the stone mattered inside. What is known is smaller: it has not been out of his plate since — not regraded, not repriced, not looked at.

pitted_silver_band.description: Thick hammered silver, tarnished and pitted all over. It was measured for a finger, and not the one it came off.
lore: A ring is the one thing in the trade that arrives with a measurement already on it. A jeweller sat down with a hand in front of him and cut this to fit it. Everything else off a broken shape has to be guessed at, but a band goes on a rod and reads off as a number, and the number was a person.

lore.t: So the crackers going through what a
Palehusk
leaves take the size before they take the price. It costs nothing and it takes a moment, and
Bettany

pays for the figures whether or not she wants the ring. She has four pages of them now. Size, date, where. Not one name against any of them and no way left of getting one, and she keeps the pages in order anyway, because a measurement is a detail, and details are the first thing to go.

lore: Eighteen gold. It is a small ring, and it did not fit.

plucked_beast_eyeball.description: Whole and damp, a brown iris in a veined tan ball. The fiends that carry spares will not miss this one.
lore: Whole or worth nothing. That is the first hard lesson of the trade and it gets learned on these, because they are the commonest eye out there and sixteen gold is real money to someone on a first bag. A burst one is a wet mark on a cloth. So you learn the spoon — the shape of it, the angle, exactly how much you can hurry and where you cannot — and you learn it at night, at the edge of a fire, from somebody who has already finished their own bag and could be asleep.

lore.t: Everyone in the trade can tell you who taught them the spoon. Not the first buyer who paid them properly, not the crossing where they lost a boot: the person who sat back down in the cold with someone else's leavings and showed them how.
Both of the trade's words
get used about this work, and neither of them covers that.

prism_tipped_quill.description: One long quill that shifts through every colour as it turns. No bird anyone has flushed grows these.

lore.t: Sixty gold buys a great many fakes. The usual method is a common quill, four dyes and a patient afternoon, and it is good enough at a lamplit stall to have taken most people at least once. The test costs nothing: turn it slowly. A dyed feather goes through its colours one at a time. A true one holds two at once, and the seam between them slides. The woman who taught
the trade
that test made the fakes for eleven years, says so freely, and is paid now to stand at the far end of the table looking bored.

purple_flower_petals.description: Purple petals with pale wedged stems, gathered past bloom. Meadow blobs trail them wherever they bounce.

lore.t: Hold one up against an
Emberwing

's wing at ten paces — closer is a mistake, and the tellers have the name of the man who tried it — and the banding matches. Violet, then the pink line, then violet again, then the pale wedge at the base where the petal leaves the stem. Not similar. The same, down to where the colour changes.

lore: Which means the wing was copied. Which means that on the other side of all this, on an afternoon nobody wrote down, a person lay on their front in a meadow with their face a hand's width from an iris and looked long enough and hard enough to keep it. They were not thinking about being remembered. They were looking at a flower. Twenty-two gold off any stall on the road, and the closest thing to a picture of one living hour that anyone here will ever hold.

purple_gold_vein_stone.description: Deep purple veined in gold, heavy as a crown. Unclaimed, which has not stopped anyone hunting for it.
lore: The names a bench uses for what a stone grades to are all borrowed from creatures: frost, ember, storm, grave, blood, moss. Point at the word and you can point at the animal. This one is filed royal, and royal is not a kind of anything — it is the word that got used because the tray needed a word. There is no creature anybody would file under it, which has not stopped two or three crews going out to look, with no description to go on and a price to go on instead.

lore.t: It does not cut. It does not burn and it will not hold anyone up. What it does is get you paid: an offer arrives a tenth over what the same bench would have said an hour before, and the man making it cannot afterwards say why, and ground you have walked twice gives up
gold
on the third pass. Nearly everything else on the shelf is an appetite or an endurance. Pressed to the bottom of this one is an expectation of being owed.

lore: Deep purple plates, thick gold in the seams, and heavy — nothing that size has any business sitting in a hand like that. Two hundred and seventy-five gold, a number arrived at by merchants, in a room, with one of these on the table. Twice a year somebody proposes a blind price: the stone in a box, in another room, valued by people who cannot see it. The proposal has never once been carried, and the men who vote it down are the men holding one.

purple_venom_claw.description: A purple hook with one pale ridge of light down the curve, and a hard green crust dried on the last third of the point.

lore.t: It grew where it sits — the one thing off an
Ashfiend

that did. Longer than a finger, curved well past use, the base a socket shaped around a knuckle that is not there any more. Hafted, it makes a poor knife every time, and people keep the poor knife, because a claw is worth little and a claw with a hand behind it is worth something.

lore: The crust on the point is the part worth money: mustard at its base, hard green at the tip, sitting on the purple rather than in it. It was put there; it did not grow there. It flakes under a thumbnail, so the careful carry one point-down in a stiff wrap and wash afterwards.

lore.t: Bettany
pays over the odds for a well-crusted one, and she is not buying knives. The same green comes off
the pale walking thing
on the black rock, and two creatures' leavings agreeing about a pigment is the kind of sentence
the Chronicle

exists to catch. Whether this point put the green into something or drew it out, the crust will not say. She keeps her best one wrapped in linen inside a chapter that has no words in it yet — just the claw, and a heading: which way did it run.

purple_void_flesh.description: A lump of violet meat that keeps twitching toward your hand. Voidmaw is mostly this, on the inside.

lore.t: No use has ever been found for it. It will not cure, will not render, will not take a dye, and it twitches toward warmth for two days and then lies still. It also carries a standing price — fifty-five,
in gold
, the same at every stall on the road — which no scrap in this trade has any business carrying. A standing price is not a fact about a lump of meat. It is a fact about somebody who wants one.

lore: A cracker off the fen followed the collection cart once, to see. Two days out, and on the second night the road he had come up was not where he had left it, so he walked home the long way. He has not sold any since; he leaves his on the stone where he finds it. He will give you his reasons at some length, and not one of them is the reason.

rainbow_tail_plume.description: Banded blue through green to red down a tan quill. Whatever grew a tail of these has not shown itself yet.

lore.t: Gunnar

measured one: quill at the base as thick as a bowstring, vane a hand and a half, and a tail wants a dozen at least before it is a tail. From that he got a span. From the span, a weight. From the weight, what a thing that size has to eat in a week and how much country that takes to find it in. He wrote the number down and he has not said it to anyone. What he will say, pushed, is that the country in question would have to be country people walk through, and that people walk through it.

raw_red_meat_slab.description: Thick, red, rimmed with brown fat. Which beast it came off is between you, the cook, and nobody else.
lore: Hunger here is a habit rather than a need, which makes ten gold of meat the strangest purchase in the trade: you are not buying food, you are buying three hours. A slab that size wants turning, and a spit wants somebody sat at it, and people who would never sit down for a telling will sit down for a plate.

lore.t: Solveig
buys the biggest she can afford rather than the best, for exactly that reason.
The newly woken

come up off the grass unable to give their own names and most of them want to walk off into the dark and be elsewhere; a person holding a plate stays where they are for as long as it takes to eat it, which is generally long enough for someone to ask them one true thing. The cooking is the courtesy. The meat is only how it gets paid for.

red_flesh_gills.description: A fan of red frills that keeps twitching after it is cut. Voidmaw breathes through a hundred of them.

lore.t: The twitch runs out along the fan and back again, and it slows on a schedule steady enough to sell. Fresh, about twice a breath. By evening, once in ten. Nothing by morning. Which makes a fan off
the ringed mouth

lying in a road a clock: something was broken here, and you can say within the hour how long ago, and from that how far ahead of you the party is and roughly what kind of day they are having. Fen-walkers read one off the ground without breaking stride. It works about as well as anything out there works, and it is the only good reason anyone has to be glad of the twitching, which is otherwise the least popular thing in the bag.

red_scaled_hide.description: A palm of deep red scales, each one overlapping the next. Emberjaw sheds them where it basks.

lore.t: Everybody who works the black rock walks on
Emberjaw

. That stone cooks a boot sole in a day and a half; a palm of red scale, cut to shape and stitched on with the overlap running heel to toe, does a season. Thirty gold, never argued, because the alternative is coming back barefoot over ground that stays warm the whole way.

lore: The cobblers read the returned soles the way other people read a road. Even wear, heel to toe: he walked in and he walked out. Worn through at the toe on both feet and nowhere else: he ran, a long way, and did not turn round to see what he was running from. There is a cobbler at the last fire who keeps the bad ones in a box under his bench. He will show you if you ask twice, and he will not give you the names, because half of them still come in for resoling.

red_seam_pyre_stone.description: Dark plates split by live red, brightest where the seams meet. It never cools, and what it sets alight keeps burning.
lore: A bag of hard pieces can be sorted in the dark if one of these is in it. Every soulstone comes out warm; this one comes out well past warm and stays there, year on year, with nothing going in. Carriers keep it wrapped and away from their backs, because after a day of it you stop being able to tell which of you is the warm one.

Setters grade by depth, against a strong light. Red that stops at the skin of the plates lights what you strike and has done; red that runs down in keeps it lit after you have moved off and stopped attending. And it will not divide — split one along its own cracks and you hold two dark rocks and no fire — so the hilt is built around the whole of it.

lore.t: A cracker once offered
Jehanne

a deep one for her rota hearth: set it in, the fire never goes out, walk the circuit in half the nights. She refused it flat, and the refusal is the nearest she comes to a creed — a fire that keeps itself is not a fire. The stone can burn. It cannot sit with anyone. She walks the full circuit still, and the coal off
the crusted thing on the black rock
goes into sword-hilts instead, where burning past reason is a virtue.

rimed_blue_soulstone.description: Grey-blue plates, white rime in every seam, cold to hold. All a Frostling's melt leaves; its hits leave a target wading.
lore: The only cold hard piece. Every other kind sits at blood heat within a breath of being picked up; this one stays cold for as long as anyone has troubled to hold it, and the sorters use that as the test — blue junk warms in the hand while you are still asking after it, a real one never does.

lore.t: The price is not about the stone; it is about the walk. The high snow lies a long way above the last fire anybody still tends, and a collector broken up there — usually by the very
Frostling
they were working — comes back together beside the nearest fire still kept, which is most often
Solveig's
on the meadow, a full day's climb below the morning's collecting, still lying in the drift where it fell.

lore: Solveig has learned the look of it: somebody assembling out of the fire-warmth at noon with snow still in their idea of themselves. She puts the kettle on and does not ask. By evening, as a rule, they are talking about going back up. Not many go up twice in a season. She has never once asked the ones who do.

rolled_grey_canvas.description: Coarse grey canvas off a Nightmule's pack, rolled tight and trailing a tail. Tents do not sew themselves.

lore.t: Open it out and it is a tent for one. Cut close, no room in it for a second set of shoulders. The original seams are double-sewn and even, the work of somebody taught properly, with time to do it right. Then, later, in different thread and in a hurry: four more tie-points added down one edge, punched through and whipped round by a hand that had plainly never done it before, so that a flap could be pegged out to the side. Somebody turned a one-man tent into a shelter for two, badly, on the road. The badly-made ties are the ones still holding. That is the whole of what is known about them — that there were two, that one of them could not sew, and that the canvas came down off
an animal that is carrying nothing at all now
and has not been pitched in a very long time.

root_web_stone.description: Brown stone threaded with living roots, taken from a Gnarloak. Leave it on soil and it takes hold.
lore: It travels on a plate. Every dealer who carries one keeps a plate for it, or a board, or a square of slate, and every apprentice is told the reason and finds it out anyway: set it down on bare soil at dusk and by morning it has taken. The stone comes up unharmed — it cannot be harmed — but you have spent an afternoon with a spade and lost a flagstone, and the man who sold it to you will not be sympathetic about either.

So there are places where somebody put one down and never came back for it. A soulstone cannot be forgotten and does not decay, so it is still there, rooted, and will still be there when the road that used to pass it has gone somewhere else. People build to those. A fire ring on the west road is laid around one, and the keepers' argument — whether the ground under it holds because of the stone or because of fifty years of people coming back to sit at it — will not be settled, and both sides keep coming back to sit at it.

lore.t: In a fight it takes a thing's feet for a moment, and that is the joke, and the trade tells it badly and often.
The creature
was assembled out of everyone's memory of a tree going over, and its last hard piece hands the axeman the one still moment he wants.
Osric
will set one for anybody who asks, at the ordinary rate, same as a buckle. He does not keep one in his own tools, and if you ask him why he will talk to you about hafts until you stop asking.

rotten_stitched_hide.description: Grey hide gone soft, with stitching still holding two ends that never matched. It smells exactly as it looks.

lore.t: It is not a hide. A saddler at the fires took one look at the seam and said so, flatly, in front of the man selling it: that is a repair. Two skins that never matched, joined with a whip-stitch worked from the inside so the mend would not show — trouble nobody takes except on a garment somebody expected to be seen in. Small stitches, a poor needle, a great deal of patience. It came off one of
the walking things on the black rock

, which is where such things end up, and the crackers price it at nine gold on account of the smell. The saddler handed his back and would not take the coin for it. He made no speech about it. He simply did not want the money, and the man who brought it in has kept it since, unsold, in a sack behind the door.

rough_brown_boulder.description: Cracked brown rock with flat faceted sides. Half the things that shed it were walking around a moment ago.

lore.t: Learn to read the flats and this stops being a rock worth four. Weather leaves a face rounded and evenly pitted. A hammer leaves a bruise with a centre to it. Teeth leave parallel scoring, wide-set, the same gauge every time, with a shallow dish where the tusk turned — and a stone scored like that is not a rock any more, it is a measurement of
Gnashjaw

's jaw, taken by the jaw. The sorters pay eleven for a clean bite and twelve if the scoring runs off the edge, because that means the animal was working on something larger and did not finish. Nothing else on the bench triples in price for having been chewed. Everything else on the bench is a piece of a creature. This is a piece of what one did.

rough_bull_hide_stone.description: Rust-brown and rough as an old hide, taken from a Tuskmaul. Warbands have broken against less.
lore: It is the one stone in a bag you can find by touch in the dark. Everything else in there comes up smooth or seamed or glassy; this is rough the whole way over, pitted and creased like a hide left out for a century, and it sets badly — it wears through leather, and a haft has to be cut deep to hold it. It does not make a person stronger. It makes them impossible to stop: once you are moving, nothing arriving from the side gets a say, not a blow, not a shove, not the ground.

lore.t: Then the part worth sitting down for. There was an age here with people enough in it, and agreement enough between them, to put a shield-wall in a field and walk it forward in step. They walked it into
the old bull

, and the wall is the part that broke. Everyone in that line re-formed beside some fire the same night, short a little of what they had been thinking, and went home, and their age went the way ages go. The agreement is gone. The wall is gone. What is left of that field sits on a bench with a price against it, warm, rough, and entirely uninterested.
Jehanne

was offered one at cost by a fire-keeper who owed her, and said no, and gave her reason at the fire that evening: a shield-wall is a rota, only larger and in a hurry, and she would rather have the rota. She keeps one. It has two names on it. It has had two names on it for a long time.

rusted_slit_stone.description: Near-black, slit all over, bright copper standing in every slit. Blows land harder and the armour that stops them fails.
lore: New hands rub the copper on a cloth, expecting the orange to come away. It never does — the first sign this is not rust in the ordinary sense — and it is warm, which rust is not. The trade grades on the copper regardless: bright, and running the full length of the slits, is a prime one; brown and pinched out is a dry one, and a dry one does noticeably less to the other man's armour.

lore.t: The odd part is that no two carry the same rust. One kind of animal, one kind of stone — there is no argument about that part — but one comes up coppery, one near black, one with a green in it, and the difference is not the animal. What pressed down in here is iron that was never its own: somebody's left-out things going off in the weather, year over year, beside
a small kept appointment
Wendell

was handed a green-tinged one at the fire a few winters back and turned it in the light a long time. The green, he said, was paint; he could name the gate it flaked off, and the wall the gate hung in. Then he talked until the fire was low, and for once — ask anyone who knows the old man — he named no price.

scaly_clawed_foot.description: Three cream claws on a brown scaled foot, cut clean at the joint. An Emberjaw's still holds its heat.

lore.t: An
Emberjaw

's foot comes off the black rock warm and stays warm, and every keeper on the cold rounds has wanted one at four in the morning. What the sellers leave out — because it is bad for business, and because it takes years to notice — is that the warmth is not a property of the foot. It is a property of how often the foot gets talked about.

lore: A keeper on the north circuit held hers hot for nine winters by telling the same story over it most nights, to whoever was sitting there: where she got it, what the animal was doing, what the rock smelled like underneath. Then she got tired of the story. She says she can close her hand round it now and feel nothing at all, and she tells people that instead, which works, and which she finds a good deal funnier than they do.

scattered_small_teeth.description: A scatter of little teeth, none of them matching. Small things lose them; smaller things collect them.
lore: Six gold the scatter, which does not cover the stooping, and every bag in the trade has some in the bottom seam regardless. You pick them up without deciding to. Then the bag goes on the counter, out they come with the sweepings, and the trader takes them by weight at a price he did not set and tips them into a barrel with everything else too small to have a name.

lore.t: Ask who buys a barrel of teeth and he will tell you the truth, which is that he has no idea. The order comes down the road, the barrel goes up it, the gold comes back, and it has worked that way longer than he has been standing there.
Bettany
has followed that road three times and come back with three answers, each of them a further stretch of road.

segmented_carapace.description: A plate of segmented shell, scuffed from digging. Dunedelver sheds them the way a road sheds gravel.

lore.t: There are still legs on it. Six or eight little dry stubs around the rim, snapped short, because a
Dunedelver

comes out of this the way a man comes out of a coat and walks off out of the leg cases as it goes. That is the whole difference between this and the rest of a bag: nothing had to be broken for it. The animal is out there right now, one size bigger, and its old back is in your hand.

lore: The trade finds that unsettling and cannot defend the feeling. A bag of teeth is a bag of endings and no one flinches at it. A carapace is a thing somebody outgrew, lying in the sand looking exactly like a leaving without being one, and there are buyers who will handle them all day and buyers who will not have them in with the rest.

severed_scaled_paw.description: Mottled grey-green hide and three pale curled claws. A Palemaw leaves them, and never in matching pairs.
lore: This is what a new cracker learns on. The hide is almost exactly the thickness of everything they will ever have to open, the joint sits where joints sit, and at thirty gold you can ruin a dozen learning where the blade goes. Three passes. You have done it right when the claws come away still hooked to one another.

lore.t: Sigrun

keeps a crate by the forge door and charges nothing for what comes out of it. She will not stand over anybody while they cut, either. What she does is ask one question, some days after their first real one, and it is not how it went and it is not what it fetched: she asks which of the two words they used about it afterwards. Everyone she has asked remembers being asked, years on, and not one of them can say precisely why it stayed.

small_horn_spur.description: A stub of horn broken off at the base. Gnashjaw grinds its tusks down and this is what falls off.

lore.t: Six gold buys a thumb of horn with a hook on the end — what comes off a
Gnashjaw

working its tusks down on a boulder — and for one season every coat at three fires on that road was fastened at the throat with one, because a man at the middle fire wore his that way and people copy.

lore: He did not start it on purpose. He had woken with nothing, the way everyone does, picked the spur off the path on his first walk out, and put it on the coat because a coat wants fastening. By the time the third fire had taken up the fashion he could no longer have told you the path or the season, and he had begun saying it had been his wife's, which it had not, and the people who knew that let him have it.

small_milk_tooth.description: A tooth the size of a fingernail, root and all. Something small lost it, and something small missed it.

lore.t: Four gold, which is the least the trade pays for anything, and there is one at nearly every fire, kept in a knot of cloth by somebody who cannot tell you what it came off. There was a man on
Wendell

's stretch of the east road who asked everyone he met the same question: do hedgehogs have milk teeth. He would produce the tooth, hold it out flat on his palm, and wait. He had had it a great deal longer than he had had the reason for it. People said yes, mostly — a
Quillkin
sheds them and they are all over the low country — and he would put it away satisfied and ask again the next season, because the asking was the part he could still lose.

smooth_black_egg.description: A smooth black egg, warm on one face and cold on the other. Every year somebody pays soulstone money for one.

lore.t: Two tests, and a new cracker has both inside a week. Put the find to the inside of the wrist and count ten:
a hard piece

is warm the whole way round, and this is warm on one face only, the other going cold against you as you count. Then set a knife-point to it. A hard piece takes no mark; this takes a grey line. Junk, then — twenty-eight gold, and worth it, because they polish, and a black one on a shelf looks like money.

lore: Which is the whole trouble. The man who works them at the ford sells to people three days woken who have heard the word and never held one, and he has never once said it. He says egg. Clearly, every time, and then waits, and lets the buyer supply the rest. He is quite right that he has not lied. The trade has a word for him anyway.

smooth_river_stone.description: Worn smooth, grey-blue and cold in the palm. Every pond blob keeps one, and none of them will say why.
lore: Four. The cheapest thing sold in Nangijala, and nearly the only one where the buyer volunteers what it is for: a hand at a fire wants a job while the mouth does the hard part, and a smooth stone is a job. The tellers keep a bowl of them by the log. At most fires you are not asked your name until you have picked one up.

lore.t: As for the
Puddlings

— a woman who spent a season at the shallows watching them says she has the answer and it is not interesting, only sad. A thing made of water needs one part of itself that stays put. Otherwise it has no way of knowing which direction is down.

smouldering_dark_egg.description: Scorched near black, embers banked in every crack. A Slagling's last warmth: it warms the blade and the hide behind it.
lore: Most hard pieces go into the bag. This one goes into a pocket, and a great many never come out again: the seams stay lit, a low orange banked down in the cracks that has never yet been seen to go out. In a blade it is a poor bargain and the trade says so — the edge runs a little warm, and that is the whole of it.

lore.t: The quarrel about them is old and fair. A teller will point out that warmth is not
a fire

— a fire is warmth with somebody talking beside it — and the two ought not to be confused. The ones who walk the black rock, where the rota lapsed further back than anyone can date and the nearest tended fire is a day down the mountain, answer that up there a warm thing in the pocket is not an argument about anything. It is company.
Jehanne
keeps fires for a living and a
Slagling's
ember in her coat, so both sides of the quarrel claim her. She lets them. A woman who prays without believing has room, she says, to be right in both directions.

soft_pastel_plume.description: A long plume shading violet to gold, softer than anything else on the stall, and off nothing anyone has seen.

lore.t: It is useless. Too soft to write with, too soft to fletch, too limp to trim a hat that would hold its shape in any wind. It has one use and it is on no list. You put it into the hand of somebody who has just woken and cannot stop shaking, because a hand holding something shakes less, and because it is the first pleasant thing this country has given them.
Jehanne
carries three, buys more than she needs, and does not call it a rite.

spiky_white_tuft.description: A burr of white fur bristling every way, blue in its shadows. Warm to wear, and slow to finish thawing.

lore.t: It comes off thorn scrub and fence wire on the passes, wherever the white things have gone through —
Winterfang

leaves it by the handful and never comes back for it. The seller at the north market has one rule and will not sell to anyone who breaks it: take a tuft bare-handed and hold it until it stops being cold. That is about a minute. The cold comes out of it into you first, all of it, before any warmth arrives, and a man who sews a hood full of it without knowing that gets an hour on the road worse than no hood at all — which is precisely the hour a cold man decides to sit down and rest a moment. Twenty gold. Half the young crackers think the minute is theatre. He lets them think so, and he still will not sell to one who lets go early.

split_bone_pile.description: Cracked long bones, split for marrow by something with no patience. Rotjaw leaves piles of them.

lore.t: A jaw splits a long bone the long way, following the grain, and leaves the halves rocking where they fell. A person splits one across, with a rock, because a person wants the marrow out and does not much care about the bone afterwards. Every guide teaches the difference in the first hour, and
Hearn
teaches it as an order: look at the split before you look at anything else.

lore: He has his reasons. A cracker new to that country came over a rise, found cracked bone scattered round a hollow, decided he was standing in somebody's camp, and sat down in it to wait for company. What came was not company. He re-formed beside a fire two nights later, short the whole afternoon and most of his reasons for being out there at all, and he tells it himself now, badly, to anyone who will sit.

spore_heart_stone.description: Dark green plates around a pale glowing core, out of a Sporehorn. The fungus is steering the stone as well.
lore: It is the only stone sold with instructions, and the seller says them out loud whether or not you want them. Do not seal it. Do not set it flush. Leave the back of the cup open, keep it somewhere light gets at it, and if the plates lift, let them lift.

lore.t: Because it is not finished. A soulstone cannot be forgotten and so cannot decay, and this one is not decaying — it is doing the other thing. Dark green plates stand slightly proud around a pale core that makes its own light, and over a season they stand a little prouder. What took
the elk

took it from the antlers down and did not stop at the bottom of it. Set it in a blade and every hit opens a small cloud that keeps working in the air behind you, which is the entire ambition of the thing steering it: arrive somewhere, and then be there.
Osric

argued about the instructions. He was a smith before he woke and he still counts in living years, and a fitting that is required to stay open offends him at a level he cannot talk himself out of, so he sealed one properly, brass over the back, to prove a point. It went dark inside four days and stayed dark. It still fights, a little. He keeps that one in his apron and brings it out when a customer wants to know why his settings cost what they cost, and he does not enjoy the demonstration as much as he pretends to.

spotted_purple_mushroom.description: Fat violet cap, pale freckles, thick lavender stem. It grows on Stumplings, which should tell you plenty.

lore.t: A
Stumpling

will stand and let you work. You can take four caps off the shoulder of one, unhurried, with it watching you do it, and it will not shift its weight the whole time — and then the basket is full, and the job is done, and the entire problem is in front of you, which is getting back out of the clearing.

lore: So watch a picker leave a wood sometime. They go backwards. Slowly, basket held to the chest, feeling behind for roots with one heel, all the way to the tree line, eyes front the whole distance. Nothing about it is dignified. Everyone who has tried it facing the other way agrees the silliness is worth twenty-four gold a cap, and they do not go into detail, and they change the subject well.

stacked_silver_bars.description: Three cast bars, stamped and stacked. Somebody smelted these, and somebody else never delivered them.

lore.t: Halvard
will weigh them, quote you low, and not move. He does not doubt the metal. It is that
gold

is the one substance everybody out of every century remembers identically, and silver is not on that list. Silver arrives arguing. His buyers came out of lives a thousand years apart and every one of them knows exactly what silver is worth, and no two of the numbers agree, and a pedlar who prices in coin and keeps walking can afford one argument a day at the outside.

lore: So a hundred and eighty gold in bars is a fortune that has to be re-agreed at every counter on the road, which is what makes the stamp worth reading. It is a house mark, not a man's name, and the house is not anywhere now. Somebody at the far end waited on a delivery that never came, and it is worth being exact about why: the bars were not lost. They are right here, three of them, stacked as they were poured. It was the road that went.

stained_marrow_bone.description: Knobbed at both ends and stained where beige should not be. A Palemaw was busy with it before you were.
lore: Six gold. The cheapest thing on the counter and the most bought, and it does not go into anybody's work — it goes in a pot.

Every fire has one on the boil most evenings. Marrow, an onion if the ground has been generous, whatever the day turned up, and it sits at the edge of the coals doing nothing urgent while the talk goes on over the top of it. Nobody at a fire has ever gone hungry, and it has never been established whether that is because of the pot.

lore.t: The stained ones — knobbed, gouged, brown where beige belongs — come off ground a
Palemaw

is working, and the crackers who bring them in scrub them and sell them and say nothing, because a bone out of that mouth boils like any other, and a stall that explains where its stock has been is a stall that stops selling.

starless_night_stone.description: Deep violet scattered with white specks, dropped by a Duskhoof. Like it, the stone casts no shadow.
lore: Put one on a windowsill in the sun. Everything else on that sill lays a shadow; beside this there is a clean bright place where a shadow should be and is not, and it will go on doing that all day, on any sill, for anybody who cares to stand and watch it. That is what makes the thing worth a hundred and fifty gold, and something else besides. It is not a story about an animal at dusk in poor light told by a man who has had a drink. It is a stone on a plank, and it holds.

On a person it works the way it works on the light. Stand still in shadow with one on you and you are not hidden so much as declined: eyes arrive, then find somewhere else to be, then go back to whatever they were doing. Moving in the dark, hands miss. Sellers state this plainly and buyers ask twice anyway, because it does not sound like a thing a stone should be able to do to a person.

lore.t: Sigrun

sets stones into steel for a living, and there is one she hands back. She takes it out of the cloth, looks at it as long as anybody does, and says she has enough work on. There is a black horse in her yard that hauls charcoal and leans its whole weight into her hand of an evening; every one of these fell out of an animal like
that one

; and she knows better than anybody at that fire what it is to put a stone into a piece of steel and then swing it every working day for the rest of your life. She has not explained herself. She is not going to.

starlit_void_stone.description: Night-black, small lights all through it, pale seams branching over it that open into nothing. Lighter than it should be.

lore.t: Handlers grade stones by heft in the dark, and this one lies to the hand: night-black, full of small lights at no settled depth, and far too light for what it is. It is the dearest thing the eastern ground gives up, and it is paid for in
gold
only — for this one, no seller takes anything that drifts.
Osric

, who had been woken about a year and still thought like a living smith, reasoned that a stone which moves a fighter might move him out of harm's way, and set one into a breastplate. It moved him one stride — into the middle of what he was backing away from. He re-formed beside
Solveig
's fire a night later, short the end of the argument he had been winning, and
Sigrun
pried the stone out of the dented plate, set it in a blade, and hung the plate on her wall where customers can see it.
In a blade, where it belongs, blows land heavy and dark, and once in a while the fight turns and you are standing on the far side of it, facing a back — the side
the Balefiend
was always on: the one you were not watching.

straw_nest_tuft.description: A knot of straw pressed into a bowl by something that slept in it. Still warm, occasionally.
lore: Sold off the same board as the tinder, worth about as much, and there is only the one selling point — which a seller demonstrates by taking your wrist and putting your hand down into the middle of it. Usually it is cold. Now and then it is not, and then you are buying a bed out from under something due back within the hour, and the price goes up rather than down, because people are people.

lore.t: Look before you let anyone put your hand in. A
Quillkin

sheds as it sleeps, the quills go in barbed and come out worse, and every dealer on that road can point you at the man who found this out in front of a crowd. He tells it himself now. He holds up the three fingers.

stretched_tan_hide.description: Pegged square with little wooden stakes, edges left ragged. Somebody began the tanning and gave up on it.

lore.t: Tanning is not difficult. It is only long: the same work, at the same hour, in the same place, for weeks — and the last part is what has gone out of this country. To peg a hide out is a promise that you will still be standing over this ground in a month, and the roads move and the fires go out.
Wendell

remembers when a hide pegged in a yard meant nothing at all: that the yard would be there next month was not a thing anyone wondered about. So half-tanned squares come into the trade constantly, and are worth fourteen gold and a shrug. Except that the pegs are still in this one. It was lifted off the ground and rolled up with its stakes, which is not what you do with a job you have given up on. It is what you do with a job you mean to finish somewhere else.

tan_down_feather.description: One soft tan feather, barbs still perfect. It came off something that flies, which narrows it down little.

lore.t: Six gold, and it takes something like four hundred to fill a bolster. Three of the four rooms at
the Long Table

are shut, and in one of them a bolster has been getting fatter for years, a handful at a time, by whoever is passing, with nobody organising it. It is not for anyone in particular. It is the bed a person would be put in, if a person came, and it is ready.

tan_sunlit_stone.description: Sand-gold and cracked like a dry bed, left by a Sunscale. It keeps the desert's noon inside it.
lore: Every hard piece comes out warm and stays warm. This one keeps a clock: cool enough to forget at first light, awkward by midday, and at the top of the day it will make you shift it off your hip — the same rise and the same fall, in a pocket, in a bag, in a cellar with no window. Sixty-two gold. Handlers who work by touch have told the hour off one and been right.

The heat does nothing; the heat is only what it is. Every so often a blow arrives as light instead of force, a white flash off the sand-gold plates, and whoever was looking at you cannot for a moment. It was never meant to last. Two seconds of somebody else's eyes, priced at the bottom of the sheet with the stones sold to people on their first road.

lore.t: Which is a failure of imagination about what is in it. People have followed
the animal

for years and come home with a colour. Nearly every stone on a bench is an appetite or an endurance — a thing that wanted, or a thing that would not stop. This one is neither. It is a way out. The plates were never armour; they were a trick played once, at the correct hour, by something whose whole answer to everything was to not be there afterwards.

lore: The crews who work the sand country carry one apiece and will tell you it is for the flash, which is true. Not one of them has ever said what they were doing at the moment they were glad of it, and every one of them has been glad of it.

tangled_cobweb.description: A torn sheet of web, still sticky at the anchor threads. Nothing in this valley admits to spinning it.
lore: Six gold, the cheapest thing in the trade, and it sells steadily all year. Ask a dealer who buys web and he will tell you: people with doors. A thread pulled across a doorway at shin height, stuck down on the tacky ends, tells you in the morning whether anything came through in the night.

lore.t: There is a man at a lapsed fire out on the western grass who strings one every evening. It has never been broken. He is not checking for what comes in: he has been
Faded

two years, he knows the order these things go in, and what he needs to know each morning is whether he went out — whether a shape stood up in the night and walked a round of the yard wearing his hands. He has begun setting a second thread at the back door, having worked out that a man in that condition would use the door he always used, and it was never the front.

teal_gold_quill.description: Teal at the base, gold at the tip, and light as nothing. Scribes want the bird; nobody has found the bird.

lore.t: Split, cut and shaved it makes a better nib than iron: it holds ink through a whole line and it does not weep in wet weather.
Bettany

has written the Chronicle with them since she began and buys every one that reaches the meadow. She has also written, at the front of each volume, in that same ink, that the entire book is being set down with a feather off an animal not one person in this country has ever seen, and that she wishes this noted. Under it, in a later hand: still no bird.

tentacled_watcher_eye.description: An eye that grew its own legs. It watched the whole fight from the floor, and it is still watching.

lore.t: Every stall that carries them carries a box with a lid, and the lid stays on while anyone at that stall is eating. Ask why and you get told bad luck, which is what the road says when it would rather not go into a thing. The plain reason is better. There are eight small eyes on the stalks and the big one in the middle, and they do not agree about where you are standing. A sorter works a bag for four hours at a stretch. Four hours is a long time to be got wrong by something on the table. Seventy-five gold, the dearest scrap off
the ringed mouth
that is not a stone, and every one of them travels face down.

thorn_vein_stone.description: Dark stone webbed in gold thorns around a green heart, off a Thornstag. Flowers die near it, indoors.
lore: It lives outside, on the sill, in a stone box. A dealer who forgets loses whatever was in the room with it — cut flowers in one night, then the herbs strung over the stove, then the pot by the window — and the standing test for a true one is exactly that and nothing cleverer. A cut stem laid beside it until morning. Sellers hand you the stem themselves. A proof that costs a flower is a cheap proof.

lore.t: Dark, gold-webbed, no trouble at all to grade. Whatever comes at you comes away torn and slower, and does not get its pace back while the fight lasts.
The stag
browses a plot down to dirt and the plot stays dirt, that year and after. One fact to a stone, pressed until it is nearly a mineral, and the fact in this one is about things not coming back.

The part worth looking at costs nothing extra. Turn it to the light and the middle of it is green — a plain grass-green heart, the same green as the stone of any leaf-eating animal on the same bench, and every thorn in the thing worked outside it. Something in that wood used to browse and mind its own business. There is no account anywhere of a Thornstag that did not read as a hole cut out of the dark: not in
the Chronicle

, not from the oldest teller anybody has been able to produce. A hundred and sixty gold, and the green middle is the entire evidence, and it cannot decay, and it cannot be forgotten, and nothing further can be added to it.

three_bright_quills.description: Three quills in blue, orange and gold, still bound together. Whatever wore them was worth looking at.

lore.t: Nothing wore all three. They are off three different somethings, and the binding is the item: a woman saw a bird once, alive, in a life she has otherwise let go of, and she has been matching its colours out of junk sacks ever since. The blue took four months. The orange is close and she knows it is not right. She brings them to
a fire
most weeks and describes the bird in order, one feather at a time, and has not yet reached the beak before the wood runs out.

tied_bone_bundle.description: Long pale bones tied off in a bundle. A Palehusk was carrying them, which raises questions about the string.
lore: Fourteen gold for the bones, which is generous, and nothing whatever for the cord, which is the part everyone actually looks at.

lore.t: A
Palehusk

was carrying it. That is not the strange part — they carry things, and going through what a broken one leaves is reading rather than robbing. The strange part is the knot. A ropemaker on the black rock road was shown one and named it without hesitating: a load-hitch, thrown left over right and dressed down, the knot you use when you mean to carry a weight a long way and want it riding quiet on your back. It is not a knot a hand arrives at by accident. Somebody was taught it.

lore: The crackers untie them. They could cut them. They untie them.

toothed_jaw_slab.description: Ivory cones socketed in a slab of jawbone, unblunted. Whatever carried it never needed a second bite.

lore.t: The first thing a buyer does is run a thumb down the cones, and what he is checking is wear. Every other tooth that reaches a counter has been used — chipped, rounded, polished on the inner face where it met its opposite for years. A slab off
a Voidmaw
comes in with the enamel still ridged from growing. Every cone a first cone. The whole ridge unopened.

lore: Twenty-eight gold, and the price is not for the ivory. It is that a jaw which never wore is a jaw that never fed, and the crackers working that ground have turned it over more than they care to. Everything else out there is doing something you could put a reason to — hungry, cold, keeping a route, waiting at a gate that is not there any more. This one has never needed a thing in its life, and it is out there anyway.

torn_brown_wing.description: A small leathery wing, torn at the trailing edge. Something flies on these; nobody has cornered it yet.

lore.t: Buyers want a pair. They always want a pair — one wing is an accident, two are a specimen — and in all the years of the trade not one honest pair has come in off the same creature. So the trade makes them. Take a big wing and a small one, trim the big one's trailing edge until the shapes agree, then rough the cut with a thumbnail so it reads as a tear. That is why so many torn wings are torn so tidily, and why a careful buyer holds the two edges up together and hunts for the same nick in both. Ten gold each, twenty-eight the pair, which tells you what the lie is worth. The whole point of
a pile of leavings
is that the details are still attached to it. This is the trade filing them off for eight gold, and the men who do it will tell you they are only giving people what they came in for.

twig_bodied_skimmer.description: Four glassy wings over a body like a snapped twig. Shaken loose from whatever swamp thing you flattened.

lore.t: The body is a stick. Not a figure of speech, and it is why the fraud is so easy: glue four wings onto
a twig

and you have twenty-two gold where you had five. Check the sockets. A real one carries four small raised collars in the shell, and you can find them with a thumbnail in the dark. Everybody in that market knows who makes the fakes. She is very good. Everybody buys hers anyway, because at twenty-two gold a fake with four real wings on it is still four real wings, and she has never once denied a thing.

violet_crystal_shard.description: A wedge of violet crystal with a white heart. Snapped off Amethyrn's crown, which it will regrow.
lore: It grows back, and that changed how it is taken. There is no sense breaking a shape that will hand you another wedge in two years, so the crown men break nothing: they come in at the shoulder while it feeds, tap once at the base with a wooden mallet, and walk out. Twice a decade, same animal. They call it husbandry and they are not entirely wrong.

lore.t: The bull

on the high pasture has been tapped nine times. It has started coming when the whistle goes. The young men take this as a compliment and tell it in company. The old ones have stopped drinking to it, because they know what it looks like when a thing keeps
walking a round
it no longer has any reason for, and this season they sent the young men up alone.

violet_eye_stone.description: A violet stone with one lidded, slit-pupilled eye that follows the room. Gloompard has four. Its stone has one.
lore: The argument at the black-wood fires is the count. Four, say the people who have met it lately, and they are not wrong. Two, say the oldest heads, who learned it before those people were dead. Six, says a man on the north side who is believed about most other things. It never settles, because everyone who has ever counted was in the dark and frightened at the time.

lore.t: Put the stones out on a bench and the argument does not end, it changes shape. Every one of them has one eye. Not a mark resembling an eye — an eye, lidded, slit through the middle, open, and tracking the room. Whatever
the animal
has been given out there, what went all the way down was a single one. A drawing is somebody's bad evening. A hundred stones in a row are a count.
Wendell

learned it with two, and gets told at the fire, kindly, that he has it muddled. He puts his stone on the table when that happens. It does not prove his number and he knows it does not; it proves the number went on from outside, that the fire has been adding to it for centuries, and that whatever the table is correcting him about, it is not the animal. He likes the quiet that follows better than he would like being right, and company is what he came for.

lore: What a buyer gets, once it is set, is the other half of the meeting: the blow that lands from behind because nothing turned to meet it, and the few seconds afterwards where the smoke has you and the field does not.

violet_hunger_stone.description: Violet and grey, a live burn of colour at the core, cut out of a Voidmaw. Set it down and the light near it goes first.

lore.t: The handlers who work the eastern ground know two stones that ought to be the same stone and are not.
The cave's

comes out cracked edge to edge with nothing in the cracks, because there was nothing left in that shape to settle. This one comes out whole: violet and grey, rough as slag, dense, heavy, with a live burn of colour at the middle that no part of a stone has any business having. That is the entire body of evidence, and it is worse than the guides' tidy answer. Something reached the bottom of
the thing

, which means there was something in there to reach the bottom of. Whatever opens that mouth is not an emptiness walking around inside a body. It is a somebody, at some level, with an appetite and no face to hang it on, and the people who take stones off that ground say so without hedging while the guide-writers go on filing it where it has always been filed.
Somebody put one in a pouch with a
banded solar stone

, as somebody was always going to. Neither stone was any different afterwards — they cannot be, that is the one thing everyone is sure of about them — but the hand's width of air between the two went out and stayed out for as long as they travelled together. Carried into a fight it takes, and hands back a tenth of what it takes, which is more than any other stone hands back to the person holding it. Nobody has ever called that generous.

violet_knot_stone.description: Violet stone cut with a knot that has no end. Scholars want it, argue over it, and cannot say what it fell out of.

lore.t: People bring this one to
Jehanne

to be read. Not valued — the scholars do the valuing, and they have bid it past two hundred and fifty on the strength of what it does, which is simple enough: whatever you can do, you can do again sooner, and it lands harder than it did the first time. What they want read is the figure. Deep violet, cut clean through with an interlace that crosses itself four times and closes, no end anywhere in it and no place where it begins.

lore: She tells them the same thing every time and it costs her a little more each time: it belongs to no rite she keeps, it is in none of her books, and she cannot say what it means. They keep coming. Belief is thin in this country and the appetite underneath it is not, and a closed figure looks so much like something meant that a man will carry it a day's walk to be told what. She knows precisely what she is being used as. She does it anyway, which is the whole of her.

lore.t: Asked a fourth time in one evening she once said more than she intended. A figure like that, she said, is what you get when a thing has gone the same round long enough that it has stopped needing anyone at the far end of it — then she got up to see to the fire, and she has not repeated it since. It is still the only reading anyone has offered, and no grader will put it on a card.
The rule everybody learns first
says something was going round. Nobody in the trade can produce it.

violet_lightning_stone.description: Violet, forked white to the shell, dropped by a Stormcrown. The air near it tastes like a coming storm.

lore.t: The sceptics' line about
the stag

is older than most of the people saying it: a tall thing on a summit in bad weather gets hit, and that is geometry, not character. A rod with legs, and the rest is people wanting a story out of a hill.

lore: The stone is the answer, and not the one they wanted. A stone carries one fact and no more, and this one's is not a thing that was struck. It is a thing that was come to. Violet plates forked white to the shell, working out from a white middle, and the hair lifts on your forearm the moment you take it up. In a fight it does not count one body a finished job: the hit lands, and then it is in the next thing along, and then it has done.

Two hundred and seventy gold, and the rest of the cost is the part nobody prices out loud. The weather that brings the lightning is the weather you have to stand in, so being broken up there is part of the errand rather than a mishap in it, and what re-forms beside the nearest tended fire is short a little of whatever it had been thinking. Ask a seller how he came by his and the answer is honest, cheerful and incomplete, and he does not know it is incomplete.

A stone cannot be forgotten. Everywhere else in the trade that is a remark about value. Up there it means something narrower: whatever else goes out of a man's head on the way down, the stone in his fist is the one part of the errand that comes back entire.

violet_mushroom_cluster.description: Three violet caps on one root, the big one freckled pale. Turn it over before you pay for it.

lore.t: Everything you are buying is on the underside. Grown in ground, the base comes up dished and full of grit. Grown on an animal — on wet moss over a shoulder that has not moved through several winters — it comes up flat, and the stems all lean one way, downhill from where the withers were. Flat is worth triple. Flat also means the picker stood near enough to a
Mireback

to take three caps off it, which is a thing a person is entitled to be proud of, and is far more often a thing a person did at home with a board and a heavy stone. Buyers know. Sellers know they know. The haggling is two people agreeing not to say so.

wheat_sheaf.description: Cut wheat bound at the waist, dry as paper. Somebody is still cutting a strip of that field every summer.

lore.t: The field grew itself, the way fields here do, out of a great many people being sure what a summer looks like. It does not need cutting. It is cut anyway, one strip a year along the north edge, by an old man with a scythe he made himself and has rehung twice. He binds at the waist, one turn and a tuck, and the collectors know his knot on sight and pay over the going rate for it, which he has never found out. Ask him why and he is perfectly clear: a field with nothing taken out of it looks wrong to him, and he would rather not look at it. He is not
thinning
. People who love him have asked, kindly, and he says so, and he is very probably right. Every year the strip is in the same place.

white_gold_branch_stone.description: White stone branching with gold light. It belongs to something that has not walked into the world yet.
lore: White going to pale blue, and the gold in it does not behave the way gold behaves in other stones. It does not lie in the seams. It branches — out of a pale middle, thinning as it travels, stopping mid-run with the ends left fine as hair. Everybody who picks one up arrives at the same word inside a minute, and the word is unfinished.

That argument is over and nobody enjoyed how it ended. Two graders on the north bench set one against a careful drawing of the same stone made ninety years before and went over it line by line, and not a hair's width had moved. Which is what a hard piece does. It cannot decay, it cannot be forgotten, and it does not become anything. So it is not growing toward something. It is finished, and exact, and it is a complete record of a kind of creature that no bench in the trade has ever put a shape to.

lore.t: Gold

is the one substance every dead person out of every century remembers identically, and a soulstone is the one thing here that cannot be forgotten at all, and there was never any reason for those two facts to end up in the same object. They are in this one, branching. Two hundred and eighty gold, and it moves slowly, to one sort of buyer: somebody who has decided to go east and would rather not say so aloud. Near it, what has been emptied does not close itself up again, and that is worth the money to them. The sellers' line — that it belongs to something which has not walked into the world yet — is repeated on every road, costs nothing, and has never been an answer to anything.

white_pebbled_snow_stone.description: Pale as packed snow, pebbled all over, dropped by a Snowmane. It walks beside whoever is lost.
lore: It will not sit on a bench. The whole surface is pebbled — packed rounds, like snow squeezed in a fist, each with its own small shine — so there is no flat anywhere on it and it goes off the edge of any table it is put down on. Sorters keep them in a cup. No other stone has a habit of leaving.

Fighters do not buy it, and the price says so: it is the cheapest honest stone anybody sells. Snow stops slowing you, cold stops counting, and that sounds like nothing until you are up where the drifts are with the last tended fire a day below you. The people who own these are carriers and rota-walkers and the ones who work the high snow for other kinds of stone, and the trade knows without saying it aloud that the cheap thing has got more people home than any of the dear ones.

lore.t: There is no way in it, whatever buyers keep hoping. What reached the bottom of
the white horse
was keeping to somebody else's pace, for as long as it takes, in weather that ought to make that impossible.
Sigrun

is a weaponsmith and will not put this one in a weapon. She sets them into boot-buckles, staff-ferrules, the tongue of a belt — evening work, and she does not charge for it — and if pressed says only that it is not blade material. She has one stone set in the head of a hammer and has had it there a long time. She is the last person in this country who needs the difference explained to her.

white_rib_cage.description: A full cage of ribs, bleached and oddly intact. It came out of something that stopped needing lungs.
lore: Everything else on the counter is in pieces. That is what junk is — the bits that came apart. A cage comes off whole, spine and sternum and every rib still seated, and it stands up on the boards looking like the one intact thing in the room, and it will not sell that way.

lore.t: Sigrun

does the same thing every time. She looks at it, sets it on the floor, puts a boot through it, and pays the man the full price for it broken.
