. Squat, heavy through the shoulder, blunt in the face, and with no interest at all in cover. It comes to a fen fire, sits down inside the light where everyone can see it, and looks at the people. One at a time. It takes as long as it takes. Then it gets up and goes back out into the dark.

lore: Hunters tell the stare as an attack, which is what people do about anything that will not stop looking at them, and the fen has a whole vocabulary for what those eyes are supposed to do to you. Watch it happen twice and the story goes flat. It is not doing anything to you. It is checking. Face, then the next face, losing interest at each one, and it has been working through faces for longer than anyone at that fire has been dead.

lore.t: Hearn

sits still for it. He is the one man on that circuit who has been looked over by something worse, and he will not say a word about that, but he will say this: you let it finish. Turning your face away from a thing that is looking for somebody is a rudeness he is not willing to commit. The others follow his lead now, so the fire goes quiet for a minute when the cat comes in, twelve people holding their chins up to be inspected by an animal, and then it leaves and they carry on.

tree_stump.description: A stump with no tree behind it, walking on root-legs. It does not mind you coming. It minds you leaving.
lore: Every village that ever was had one: the stump at the wood's edge where you walked people to say goodbye. You carried their bag that far and no farther, and they sat on it to retie a boot, and then they went, and you stood by the stump until you could not see them. A thousand villages, a hundred thousand goodbyes, all of them remembered hard by the people left standing there — and in Nangijala that much remembering, pooled in one shape, eventually stands up.

So mind the one thing every handler tells you and no field guide bothers to: a Stumpling will let you walk right up. It goes for your back. The lashing starts when you turn and go, because going is the only thing that was ever done to it, and somewhere in all that borrowed remembering it has decided, wordlessly, with nobody inside it to decide, that this time it will not be left.

lore.t: Sigrun
will not crack them. She does the trade's other work all day and charges double to anyone who brings her one of these still whole, hoping she'll change her mind. The stone inside is
blood-natured

— it feeds your wounds shut while you fight, holding on to you the way the stump holds on to everyone — and she says a thing that keeps its grip that well should be allowed to keep it. People assume she is joking. People have not watched her leave her smithy, at the end of a market day, by the long way around the one that stands at the east fence.

undead_charger.description: It would not fall when its rider did. It still charges a line that is not there, in horns no horse ever grew.
lore: Nothing that ever grazed a field had that head. A horse's skull as far as the brow, then two great curled ram's horns on it, a ridge of bare spine standing out of the hide, something red down in the sockets. It did not look like that in life. It looks like that because it was the last thing a great many frightened men saw properly, and frightened men are poor witnesses, and enough of them told it the same way for long enough that the telling won. Set in the bone above the eyes is a small gold boss, all that is left of a head-piece somebody buckled onto it every working morning.

lore.t: The war is in nobody's book.
Bettany

has asked at every fire on her circuit for a banner, a year, a river, a reason, and come back with none of it — everyone who could have told it has gone Quiet, and it was never told often enough to hold. What survives of the entire business is one horse that will not stop, and a set of horns it never had.

It does not charge people. It charges lines. Two of you standing together are furniture; six in a row are a shield-wall, and it comes at the middle of the row at a flat gallop and does not check. Most of the work at a fire is done in rows — wood passed hand to hand, buckets, a line walking the ground abreast at first light.
Hearn

teaches everyone who works that country the same three sentences, and teaches them as orders, because an order is the only way he knows to say a thing fast enough. Break up. Stand apart. It is not coming for you, it is coming for the row.

undead_hound.description: A dog that would not stop waiting. Its crooked jaw hangs loose, grinning at a joke told before it came.
lore: The joke was not funny. A long one about a neighbour and a borrowed ladder, with the same wrong pause in the middle every time, told to the same dog most evenings for nine years by a hill farmer with no one else to try it on. The dog did not have the joke. The dog had the last two seconds of it: the man's own laugh going off like a dropped pan, a hand coming down heavy on its head, then supper. That is a complete world, if you are a dog.

lore.t: Then the farmer's turn came, and the dog's came after, and the dog
woke in the meadow grass

like everything else that arrives here. It waited. He was not there, and he was not there the next season, and past a certain point the word for a man like that is the heaviest one in the language: he is one of the unwoken.

lore: A dog cannot draw a conclusion from that. It is the only mercy in the business.

So it waits at the head of any track that climbs toward a farm — hide gone patchy, ribs standing out, something green lifting off its spine in the cold — and through all of it the jaw has not slipped a hair, hung open and crooked and full of teeth, fixed in the two seconds before a hand comes down. People have tried feeding it. It is not hungry. It wants the two seconds.

water_poring.description: Two big eyes in a wobble of pond water. Corner it and it bursts into spray, then gathers itself back up.
lore: No creature drowned to make the ponds' one. A low wet place got remembered by a great many people and visited by none of them, and the remembering pooled the way water pools, and one morning it had a face. Fight it and it bursts — alarming exactly once — sits a moment as a flat wet patch, and is a blob again before you have decided how you feel about that. Nothing lands. There is nothing in it to land on.

lore.t: The sorters' first question for any wild thing — what has it lost? — goes nowhere here, which is exactly why
Bettany

carried her whole list down to the pond and put every question to one aloud, in order, while it wobbled and watched her. It burst once, when a heron came down, and was back before she had finished the next question. Under its page in
the Chronicle
she wrote: stayed to the end of the questions, which is more than most people do. She maintains that this was an observation.
The pond, for what it is worth, has not moved since. Two Turns have been through the low country and left it exactly where her page says it is.
Gunnar
marks it on his maps as the stillest water in the district and, being Gunnar, will not say why he thinks so.

white_horse.description: White as the morning it vanished from the king's stable. It allows no rider, but walks beside the lost.

lore.t: In life it was somebody's, and expensive, and one morning the stall stood empty with the door still bolted. That story is presumably still being told wrong in the living country. The truth is the ordinary one: it came the way everyone comes,
woke in the meadow grass
, and has no idea it is supposed to be a wonder.

lore: It will not be ridden and has never once made a fight of it. Put a saddle on and it stands patiently through the girth and the buckles; get a leg across and it simply walks out from under the whole arrangement and leaves you holding tack in an empty field. There is nothing there to argue with. Nothing was refused.

What it does instead is walk beside people who are lost — at the shoulder, at exactly their pace, for as long as it takes. Several have tried following it, on the reasonable assumption that a horse doing that must know a way, and been walked in a wide meandering circle back to their own footprints, because it was never leading. It goes where you go. All it does is see to it that a person alone in the dark is a person and a horse.

lore.t: Solveig

sees it more than anyone. Somebody comes stumbling in out of the dark towards the meadow fire with a white horse at their shoulder, and at the edge of the light the horse stops, and turns, and goes back out. It will not come in to the warm. The one courtesy she has never managed to do is thank it.

white_rabbit.description: Tame in a way nothing wild is: it comes closer than it should, bolts, and bites in earnest when it cannot run.
lore: White is a poor colour in country that has things hunting in it, and the coat is not the strange part. The strange part is that it comes toward you. Nothing wild does that. A rabbit has decided in advance about every noise there is, and this one decides right about all of them, and then for a moment decides wrong: three or four steps in your direction, ears up, the way an animal moves toward a person it is expecting — then whatever is left inside catches up with it, and it is forty feet away. Somebody kept this one. The somebody got forgotten before the rabbit did.

lore.t: Twice a day it comes out onto the same patch of open ground within sight of
the meadow
, faces the same way, and waits. Nothing arrives.
Solveig

can see the spot from the fire, and when the fire can spare her she goes and sits at it — a little way off, at the hour, saying nothing. It will not take food from her; she is the wrong person, and it knows that better than it knows anything. She goes anyway. She has met strangers at their worst hour her whole watch, and she says a kept hour should not have to be kept alone.

lore: It will not turn while it still has somewhere to run. Take that away and it turns, and the teeth were always real. Most first seasons include this lesson, the gentlest on offer: nearly everything in this country will hurt you eventually, and almost none of it means to.

blood_spatter.description: A stain is a story that ended at the nearest fire. Almost always.
lore: Fights end. The broken go down where they stand and, some hours on, stand up again beside the nearest tended fire, short a little of whatever they were thinking when it happened. That is the arithmetic of violence here: it costs a thought, not a life. So a stain on the stones is not a marker. It is the start of a story that finished somewhere warmer — an argument gone too far, a robbery on the road, a creature that had to be released the hard way — and by the time the rain gets around to it, the person it came out of has usually walked past it twice without looking down.

lore.t: Usually. The re-forming needs a tended fire, and the rota has lapsed almost everywhere. Out where the map has gone
Quiet
, the nearest fire can be a long way to nowhere. The old hands read stains the way trackers read prints: fresh means a scuffle. Faded, far from any light, means don't ask.

campfire.description: The fire on the meadow. It has never once been let go out.

lore.t: It has never gone out. That is not a figure of speech: it is the fire Signe lit, or a fire fed from it, or a fire people only say was fed from it, and in this country all three are the same wood. Every soul that ever opened its eyes on the meadow saw this light first — before the stone house, before the grass, before their own name came back to them.
The waking
is cold and confused everywhere except within reach of it.
Solveig

keeps it now. There is a seat with its back to the wind, a second cup in case the newest arrival comes thirsty, and split wood stacked like a promise. When she asks your name and one true thing, look into the flames while you answer; everyone does. What is said there holds.

lore: Feed it if you pass. Not because it needs you tonight — because one night it will, and it does not announce which.

grave_cross.description: A cross over no grave, raised for someone who never woke.
lore: Nothing is buried under it. Nothing is ever buried here: the Quiet leaves no body, no bone, no weight for a shovel. A grave is a living country's answer to a problem this one does not have.

lore.t: The crosses are for the other absence. People die together — a sickness, a wreck, a winter — and one of them wakes on the meadow and the other never comes.
The waking

owes no explanation and gives none. So the woken do the one thing left to do: they cut two pieces of wood, plant them where the missing one would have been welcome, and say the name aloud, on the old understanding that what is spoken holds. It is the only telling in Nangijala that does not work. The name holds nothing, because the person it belongs to is not here to be held. They say it anyway. Every cross on the map is somebody still saying it.

entries.name: The Waking
entries.summary: You died. Then you woke on a meadow, and a stranger was already walking toward you. This chapter is about her, and about the ones nobody got to meet.
body: Nobody remembers the door. You were somewhere else, at the end of something, and then you were lying in meadow grass with your face wet and the smell of woodsmoke coming from somewhere close, and every person who has ever lived in Nangijala began exactly there — on that meadow, within sight of that small stone house, within reach of that fire. The country has one gate and it is a field.

body.t: You will not know your own name. This frightens people more than the dying did. The name is not taken; it just does not always survive the crossing, and a woken soul will sit in the grass for an hour reaching for it the way you reach for a word you have used all your life. Which is why the first thing you see here is not the sky and not the house. It is
Solveig
, already walking toward you, because she watches the grass the way sailors watch weather, and she can tell a waking from a trick of the wind at three hundred paces.

body: She will sit down a little way off, so you can look at her or not. She will tell you what happened to you, plainly, once, because she has learned that kindness with the truth left out has to be done twice. And before you sleep she will ask you for your name, if it has come back, and one true thing about yourself, and she will listen to your answer like it is the only thing happening in the world. It is not a ritual, though it has been done a hundred thousand times. It is the oldest medicine this country has, and you will learn why it works soon enough.

She was not the first to keep that watch. The fire on the meadow is older than any person now tending it, and the ones who kept it before her are a story she will not tell on a first evening — partly because you are not ready, and partly because one part of it she cannot tell without stopping, and she does not stop while she is on watch.
Here is the part she will tell you, because you have to know it and it is better from her than from the wall of some tavern. Sit down for it.
Not everyone comes.

People die together — in the same water, on the same road, in the same winter — and one of them wakes on the meadow and the other never does. Husbands arrive and stand up already scanning the grass for a wife who died eleven years before them, and she is not here, and she was never here, and no one can say where else there is. The woken keep lists. They describe faces to Solveig, to travellers, to anyone who has walked far: have you met her, she would have come the year of the great storm, she laughs before the joke is finished. There is a whole quiet economy of people asking, and the country has never once produced an answer — only the fact, repeated until everyone stops asking out loud: some of the dead never wake, and nobody knows what that means, and everybody is afraid that somebody does.

So when you stand up out of the grass, understand what the woman at the fire is actually doing. She is not staffing a gate. Every waking she meets is somebody's answered prayer — the person a hundred strangers have described to her, finally face-up in the grass — or else it is one more day that somebody's person did not come. She meets you anyway, full-hearted, every time. Ask her how she bears the arithmetic and she will feed the fire and say the watch is the watch.
Welcome to Nangijala. You are dead, you are expected, and you are — this is the strangest part, and it takes everyone a season to believe it — not at the end of anything.

entries.name: The Age of Coming
entries.summary: The ruins of the first age had owners: a lighthouse lit for a brother who never woke, a mill brought by a woman who hated it, a face nobody can ask about — and then the first wall went soft.

body.t: Walk east from
the meadow

for an afternoon and you will pass under a broken aqueduct, through a ring of standing stones, past a windmill with its sails still rigged, and along a line of poles strung with wire that runs from nowhere to nowhere. None of these things belong in the same world. All of them are here.

body: The dead arrive from everywhere and every when, and here remembering is not a private event: a thing held firmly enough, long enough, in enough minds, simply is. Somebody woke knowing exactly what an aqueduct was — knew it the way you know the stairs of your childhood house — and so there is an aqueduct. The oldest call that first stretch of the world's history the Age of Coming. No maintenance, no scarcity, nobody yet suspecting that anything needed keeping; the country grew larger, stranger and more beautiful, and nearly everything good to look at dates from it. But the ruins are not the lesson. The lesson is the people they belonged to. Meet three of them.

The lighthouse stands in the shallows of a sea no ship has ever crossed, and a man named Nils built it with his hands. In life his brother drowned within sight of a real one — lamp lit, keeper awake, the whole machinery of warning working exactly as intended, and his brother slipping under quietly a little way outside the light. Nils died years later, far from any coast, and woke on the meadow still listening for water. On a shore with nothing to warn he built a lighthouse anyway, and then he changed what a lighthouse is for: he lit it every evening, so that if his brother ever woke in this country — on the meadow, in the far hills, anywhere — there would be a light on the water that meant: come here. I kept it burning. His brother never woke. Nils lit the lamp anyway, every evening, for longer than most countries last, because he would not agree that it was for nobody. The lamp is cold now. The tower stands.

The windmill nobody turns was brought by a woman who hated it. She had been put to it as a girl — wind, grain, the same circle of sky — and she walked out of its shadow the day she was grown and never once looked back. She lived, she grew old somewhere with pavement under her feet, she died, she woke on the meadow. Within a season the sails stood up over the birches, because the Age of Coming never asked what you loved. It asked what you knew all the way to the bone, and what she knew, under everything she built on top of it, was the mill. She spent a long age here in its shadow, furious. You do not choose what comes with you. You are not asked.

And out on the ice there is a statue with a face nobody recognises. It was carried here on somebody's back, the whole way, over years; people still tell of the carrier on the roads, bent double, refusing carts, refusing company, setting the burden down at dusk and sitting opposite it in silence until dark. Nobody asked. Asking felt like putting a finger in a wound. Now the carrier is long gone from every road, there is no one left to ask, and the statue stands in the ice being the most important face in somebody's world — name unknown, story unknown, kept upright, the old ones say, by the wondering itself, because ten thousand travellers asking whose face is that, at ten thousand fires, is also a kind of remembering. Whoever it was is held in the world by strangers. That is either the loneliest thing in this chapter or the kindest, and nobody has settled it.

The age ended without ceremony. A man had set a triumphal arch in a field, for a victory won in a country that is not here, and for a long lifetime he told that victory to anyone who slowed down — until one year he stopped, because everyone had heard it. The carved faces on the arch went smooth first, like wax near a flame. Then a wall somewhere was not as tall as it had been, and then it was a heap, and then a green place where a heap used to be. Whole streets began to be less. Nobody understood. They blamed the winters, they blamed the ground, and there was a whole confident generation certain it had something to do with the sea.

body.t: It had nothing to do with the sea. The answer was paid for by one silent woman, and what it cost her is
the Age of Fires

entries.name: The Age of Fires
entries.summary: Signe learned the world's rule by losing Emil to her own silence. The first fire, the rota as an apology to a boy who cannot hear it, and the argument between telling and writing that nobody has won.
body: Before the rule had words, somebody paid for it. A woman called Signe woke early in the world's history, when the country was young and nobody yet knew it needed keeping, and the first thing Nangijala ever gave her was the sound of her boy laughing on the far side of the meadow. Emil. He had gone through the ice at seven; she had carried that for years, and then followed; and here he was, running at her through the grass, still seven, still hers.

Signe was not a talker. That is the whole tragedy in one line. She loved enormously and said almost none of it, on the old reasoning that a thing said aloud gets smaller. She sat with her boy inside a silence she believed was full. Love that says nothing had never cost anyone anything.

Then Emil began to thin. Slower to name things, at first — the stream became the water, and then he only pointed. Then slower to be named: neighbours' eyes went past him, and a traveller once asked Signe, kindly, whether she lived alone. She did what silent people do. She gripped harder and said less. She held his hand on every walk and told nobody so much as his name, because saying it aloud would have made it real.

body.t: He went
Quiet

holding her hand. There was no moment to point to. The hand was in hers, and then the hand was empty, and the place where he had been was slightly wider than it should have been. She had lost him twice now. The second time was her fault, and the fault was silence, and she did not know either of those things yet.

body: She did not speak for a season. It began as mourning and ended as the coldest experiment this country has ever run: while she sat in it, the world went soft around her. The path they had walked lost its far end. The gate he had swung on stood less certainly on its hinges. Everything nobody spoke of was leaving, and she recognised the weather — it was the one that had taken her son. The discovery was not an insight. It was an autopsy.
The things people talk about stay.
And the half of it that was hers to keep: a boy who went through the ice at seven is talked about by his mother, or by nobody.

So she lit a fire, because you cannot make people sit and listen in the dark and the cold, and listening, it turns out, is the whole medicine. Then the woman who had said almost nothing across two lives sat a stranger down and told him about Emil — the winter, the ice, what his voice did to a room — until her own voice went, and the stranger listened until it was done, and around that one fire the world firmed up like ground after frost. What is told aloud, to somebody listening, holds. It was the world's one law, found too late for the only person she wanted it for.

body.t: What grew from that evening is called the Age of Fires, and it was the best of us. Fires, and a rota: somebody answerable for every fire, somebody walking the circuit between them carrying names, somebody meeting every waking to ask a name and one true thing while somebody else listened. They call the whole of it the Keeping. And every part of it — the rota, the fires, the questions
Solveig
asked you at
your own waking
— is Signe's apology to a boy who cannot hear it. This country runs on love that arrived too late and refuses to stop arriving.

The argument came later, and it has a knife in it. A told story grows — retold a little warmer, a little braver, a little better shaped, by people who mean nothing but well. Keep a man alive by telling him for forty years and you have a man: solid, present, going nowhere, and not quite the man who fell. The Fire-Keepers call that the price. So the Chroniclers said: write him down, exactly, once, and he is safe from all of you and your warmth. They were right and thorough —
the Chronicle
is their book;
Bettany

writes it now — and then they found the thing nobody has explained. A person recorded perfectly goes Quiet anyway, on the usual schedule, beside their own complete and accurate account. It was never the accuracy, the Fire-Keepers say; it was the listening. That is not an explanation, the Chroniclers say; it is a slogan. Nobody has won. You will be asked.
As for Signe: she never forgave herself, and she never
went on

. Late in her age, people who knew her said the two had grown into each other until she could not tell them apart — staying had become the apology. Then the record thins, the way records here do, and what became of her is not written. Not in this book. Not in any teller's round. The woman who taught the world its keeping was not, herself, kept.
But the fire on the meadow — the one you woke within sight of, the one
Solveig

feeds tonight — has never once been let go out. Underneath everything this country still does, every name asked and every true thing listened to, there is a woman saying to a boy, too late, in the only language she ever managed: I am still here.

entries.name: The Quiet
entries.summary: Nothing here dies. It thins — Bright, Faded, Habit, Quiet. You learn the stages the way everyone does: from outside, beside Wendell on the east road, visiting somebody who is no longer home.
body: You cannot die in Nangijala. That door is behind you and it does not open twice. The newly woken find this reassuring for about a season.

It does not mean nothing can happen to you. You can be broken — knocked past the point of holding a shape — as unpleasant as it sounds, and not an ending. What is left of you goes where the remembering is thickest, in practice the nearest tended fire, and puts itself back together beside it over a few hours. You keep what you were carrying. You lose a little of what you were thinking about. Nobody here treats a fight as final, and everybody knows exactly how far it is to the nearest lit fire.

body.t: What can still happen to you is slower, and a list of stages will not teach it to you. You learn it watching somebody you love. So learn it from
Wendell

, the oldest head at the meadow fire, who pays for his suppers with the east road — the carts, the inn at the ford, the summer the verge came up in flowers, all from when the road was safe. People trade him a listening for an evening of it and think they are being kind to an old man. Then, when the weather is quiet, Wendell walks that road himself, out past where anybody goes now, to visit somebody.

body: Thinning has four stages, called the same four things since anybody started counting: Bright, Faded, Habit, Quiet. None of it hurts. That is the part people find hard to hear.

Bright is what you are now. You know who you were and you can say it — your name, your work, the face of somebody you loved, the road home. The one he visits was Bright a long time. She told the east road better than he does; he learned it from her. He does not say what she was to him. Nobody asks twice.

Then you Fade. The particulars go first, so gently nobody catches them leaving. She knew she had loved people; she could not produce the faces. She knew the road went somewhere, and no longer which way it ran. A Faded person is still entirely present, with less and less to say about it, and it is the stage where saying them back to themselves, out loud, at a fire, still takes. Wendell did that for years. Some evenings it worked, and those were the worst ones, he says, because of what they let him hope.

Then there is Habit, where it stops being sad and starts being frightening: the person is gone and the behaviour is still running, a shape walking its round with nobody home. She walks the east road now. The same stretch, out and back, at the hour she always walked it. Wendell falls in step beside her. He gives her back her own stories at walking pace, the carts, the ford, the flowering summer, and she does not stop, and he does not stop either, and when the light goes he stands still in the road and lets her walk away from him.

body.t: Count what the old man is doing before you call it sentiment. A shape at Habit holds only as long as its round holds, and a road nobody speaks of goes soft like everything else. So he sells the east road to the fireside, one listening at a time, keeping it firm under her feet. And he walks beside her so that anybody who comes out that way with a hammer, meaning the quick mercy the trade deals Habit shapes, finds an old man standing in the road first. What the trade does is
the next chapter
. Wendell has read it. He has an opinion about mercy.

body: Carry her with you among the wild things, because nearly everything out there is at Habit too. The creatures are not wicked. Some outlasted their occupants, some never had one at all, and either way they come at you for reasons that stopped being reasons long ago — a round still walked, a bridge still guarded for a keeper whose name went out of the world before it did. Do not hate them. Every one of them is somebody's east road.

And at the end, the Quiet. The shape lets go. There is no body and no grave, because there was no death; the thing simply stops being anywhere, and afterwards the place it was seems slightly wider than it should. People who have watched say the worst part is how ordinary it looks. Wendell has watched. The worst part, he says, is that the road will still be there.

The Quiet is what this world is afraid of — not the creatures, not the cave, not the winter. Every fire, every rota, every supper an old man buys with a dead road is the same answer to the same question. Nobody says the question out loud. It walks the east road on the quiet evenings, at the pace of an empty shape, an old man keeping up, saying carts, saying ford, saying flowers.
Who is going to remember me, and will they do it out loud.

entries.name: The Hard Pieces
entries.summary: What a soulstone is, and the trade's two words for taking one — told through Sigrun, who released her own husband rather than let a stranger crack him, and has not said his name since.
body: Everything that thins gets thinner all the way down, and then stops. At the very bottom one thing refuses to go any further, and if the shape is broken open it falls out into the grass. It is about the size of an egg. It is warm.

body.t: This is a soulstone. It is not a soul — a soul is a whole person, and no person fits in a stone. What is in there is the last piece: one fact, one appetite, one habit of being, pressed down over centuries until it is very nearly a mineral. A thing that spent itself burning leaves a stone that is still, in some stubborn way, about burning. A thing that endured cold leaves a stone that endures it. One kind of creature, one kind of stone, no exceptions — except near the eastern mountain, where what the broken things leave behind is
another matter

body: Because a soulstone cannot be forgotten, it cannot decay, and in a country where everything else is quietly going soft that makes it the most valuable substance there is. Work one into a blade or set it into armour and it lends you a little of what it remembers. It does not make you stronger. It makes you harder to argue with.
The people who take stones out of thinned shapes for a living have two words for the work, and everything worth knowing about any of them is in which word they use.

The polite word is releasing. It is not dishonest. A shape at Habit has nobody left inside; it is going to let go regardless, in fifty years or five hundred, and everything it still carries will go with it — except the stone, if somebody saves the stone. Put like that it is a mercy, and some of the people who do it have thought it through with care and concluded exactly that.
The other word is cracking. It is what the same people say to each other, over drink, when the bag is heavy and the mercy has been done nine times since breakfast.

body.t: The whole distance between those two words is one person wide. She stands at a forge, and her name is
Sigrun
Sigrun is the weaponsmith. Her husband thinned. She watched it go the way
the last chapter

says it goes — Bright, then Faded, then one morning there was a shape at her door wearing his hands, running the one habit of him that was left. She knew the trade. She knew what a wandering Habit shape is worth, how soon somebody with a good eye would find him on a road somewhere, and which of the two words that stranger would use about it afterwards, over drink.

body: So she shut the forge and went out to him herself. One blow. Hers.

His stone is set into the head of her hammer, and it has been in the striking of everything she has made since — every blade she sells has him somewhere in it. Buyers say her steel keeps its edge longer than steel should, and she lets them say it. She calls what she did releasing, and she has earned the word, and nobody in the trade uses either word carelessly where she can hear.

body.t: What she has not done, from that morning to this one, is say his name. Not at the fire. Not to the Chronicle —
Bettany

asked once, gently, and there is no record of a second asking. Sigrun knows, better than anyone, what this country does to a name nobody says aloud. She has not said it anyway. Understand why, and you understand both words, and you are as ready as anybody ever is to pick a warm stone up out of the grass.

body: The rest of what comes off a broken shape — teeth, hide, bone, feathers, a knife somebody was still carrying — is junk, worth almost nothing and collected by absolutely everybody, because a pile of leavings is a story with the details still attached, and details are what go first. And somebody, somewhere, is buying every scrap of it, and has been for a long time, and has never once explained what for.

entries.name: The Gold Agreement
entries.summary: Gold is the only thing everybody remembers the same — the one inheritance that crosses. Coins left on woodpiles against debts nobody is collecting, and a widower still paying into a plan for two.
body: Nangijala never decided on money. There was no mint, no decree, nobody with the authority to bind a country whose people arrive from every century at once. What happened is that somebody noticed a fact about gold, and the fact did the rest.

Gold is the only thing everybody remembers the same. Everything else arrives arguing: two of the woken, from lives a thousand years apart, will give you two roads, two loaves, two kings, all of them real, disagreeing in the same field forever. Ask them both for a gold coin and you get the same coin — the weight, the colour, the soft way it takes the mark of a thumbnail. On that one point the whole of human memory closes like a hand. So a coin never drifts and never goes soft. Everything else you own is held in shape by somebody's attention; a coin holds with nobody holding it. Money, by discovery.

body.t: Which makes gold the one inheritance that reliably crosses. Your house did not come with you. Your tools, your deeds, your letters did not. Your face barely did. But a coin you knew — the one sewn into your coat, the one you were paid the morning you died — is in your pocket on
the meadow
, exact to the scratch, and
Halvard

, who walks his pack between the fires, takes it without one question. He prices everything in gold and trusts nothing else to still be itself by morning; his customers died centuries apart, and the coin is the only thing all of them agree about. He has learned to stand inside that agreement and trade.
Watch what the woken actually do with gold, though, and it is rarely buying. The new ones keep trying to pay for things that have no price.
Osric
, woken only weeks and still counting in living years, tried to pay
Solveig

for his first night beside the meadow fire; she told him the fire is not for sale; he waited until her back was turned and left the coin on the woodpile anyway, because he could not sleep owing. People leave coins here the way the living leave flowers — on a doorstep that was kind, on the sill of the stone house, beside fires they cannot stay to feed. It is not commerce. It is the habit of squaring things, carried across by people who owe nothing now, and it will not leave them.

body: And at one of the eastern fires there is a man who pays Halvard a coin at every visit and buys nothing. In life he and his wife put a coin by every market day, toward a house with a south window. She died first. She never woke here, and he does not know what that means — nobody does — so he keeps the only part of the plan still in his power, which is the putting-by. Halvard carries the count in his book, one long column with nothing against it, and once, gently, he tried to hand it all back. Only once.

entries.name: The Long Morning
entries.summary: The way out is open to everyone, costs nothing, and almost nobody takes it. When somebody does, the grief of those left behind goes missing. Bettany braced for hers and was robbed of it instead.
body: Nangijala is not the last place. That much is not in dispute, which makes it unusual among everything else in this book.

Every so often somebody here stops being here. Not the Quiet — nothing like the Quiet. A person who is entirely Bright, all the way back to their own name and their own face, needing nobody to hold any piece of them, will one evening simply not be in the room. That night the northern sky lights up. The tellers say the lights are the far edge of somebody else's dawn, seen from underneath. It is a beautiful thing to say. Nobody has come back to confirm it. Not once, not ever, not a word.

The way is open to everybody and it appears to cost nothing. Remember yourself completely and you may go on. That is the requirement, the only requirement, and it has never once been observed to fail. And almost nobody goes. To understand this country you have to hold both halves of that sentence, and the second half begins with the people left in the room.

body.t: When Britt went on — young in death, bright as a coin, whole faster than anyone the tellers could name — her sister braced for the grief the way you brace for cold water.
Bettany

is a scribe; she had done grief before, she knew the shape of her own. It never came. She remembers Britt entire — every year, every fight, the exact pitch of her singing over the wash-water — and she has never found one grain of sorrow in herself, not that night, not since. That is what broke her. Not the loss. The absence of the loss. Grief was the last thing of her sister she owned, and something took it.

Everyone bereaved by the Long Morning reports the same absence, and nearly everyone else calls it a mercy: see how gently the country lets go of its best. The bereaved learn to stop answering that. What it is like — Bettany has collected the testimony, and the wording barely varies — is coming home on the day of the funeral to find the house has been entered and exactly one thing taken, and everything else left neat, and the neighbours saying what a kind thief. She refuses to call it mercy until somebody can tell her what it is. She began
the Chronicle
to find out. You are holding it.

body: So the question the woken always ask, a year in, at somebody's fire, wearing the face of a person who has spotted what everybody else missed: if the door is open, and it costs nothing, why is anybody still here?

body.t: Walk the country and the answers are standing at their posts. A woman comes to the meadow for every waking because her husband has not fallen yet, and she will not go on ahead of him, and she has waited long enough now that the waiting has begun to replace her. A man on the eastern fells follows, at a distance, a shape gone to Habit that used to be his brother, walking its one faithful empty round; he will not leave a thing that still has his name in its mouth.
Hearn
came back from
the hole under the mountain
alone, the only one of that company who did, and going on has looked to him like getting away with it ever since; he stays, and does not get away with it, one deliberate year at a time.
Jehanne
keeps every form of a faith she stopped believing, and will not walk toward a far shore she cannot pray to; she has given up arrivals, she says, and will not be caught hoping. And
Solveig
could go any evening she chose — she is as whole as anyone in this country — and every evening she chooses the fire, because if she goes, who meets them?

body: Ask anybody in Nangijala why they are still here and they will tell you, if you have sat with them long enough. Everybody has an answer. It is the answer that makes them a person rather than a shape. Sooner or later you will find out what yours is.

entries.name: The Hole Under the Mountain
entries.summary: Eleven masks on one table: one face, all smiling. The hole is new, and the oldest say the worst part is who it must have been. It is hungry, not hateful. One man came back: it asked politely.
body: Everything else in this book is the world working as it always has. This chapter is the exception. Read it, and then do not go east.

There is a cave under the eastern mountain. One mouth, not hidden; every person in Nangijala can tell you roughly where it is. Nobody ever needed a legend to find it. The whole difficulty runs the other way.

body.t: Near it, things forget faster. That was measured carefully, by people who wanted it to be wrong: ground held for centuries — in the rota, with a fire on it — went soft in a season, and then the season became a month. A keeper on the eastern circuit lost the name of her own fire walking toward the mouth and had it back within the hour of walking away, and she was not a woman anyone had known to lose anything.
Gunnar
, who maps the Drift, still walks the eastern line every year. He has stopped telling anybody what he measures.
Out in the wild a beast is
a shape that outlasted whoever was in it

, running on habit, empty, wanting almost nothing from you. The creatures near the mouth are not that. They were not left empty — they were emptied, all at once, and something else is wearing the outside. The word is Hollowed. The trade will not take money to touch them.
Break one and a mask comes down out of it and lands in the dirt, still smiling — the little dark
Grinmask

is the one most often seen to drop one. A mask does not thin. It lies in the grass being exactly a face after everything else has stopped being anywhere at all. For years the comfortable explanation was that a face is simply the last part of a person to let go of — the piece the emptying could not take. Then
Bettany
borrowed every mask anyone had kept — eleven, from eleven creatures broken years and miles apart — and laid them out in a row on one table.

body: They are the same face.

Not eleven faces that happen to be alike. One face, eleven times, the way eleven drawings by eleven hands of one person are one face — never quite agreeing, unmistakably the same attempt. No straps, no eye-holes, no wear. Nothing ever wore these. They were made, one after another, by something that keeps missing what it reaches for by a width nobody can name. Except the smile. The smile is identical on all eleven. Nobody says the comfortable thing any more.

body.t: There has been one organised attempt on the cave. One, ever. The best the fires had went in on a summer morning, and in the evening
Hearn
came back out alone, unhollowed, unmarked. Everyone has asked him what is inside — the kind, the cruel, the drunk,
Bettany

with her book open — and all of them got the same three words: it asked politely. He buys rounds he cannot afford for people who are not there to drink them. The others never re-formed at any fire anybody keeps, and nobody who walks the east road at dusk looks closely at the shapes they pass, in case of knowing a walk.
Two things are checkable, and they are the worst facts in this book. The first: the hole is new. Not new the way a season is new — new the way a wound is. The
Age of Fires
had no hole under the eastern mountain.
Wendell

was already old when the east road was just a road, and for an evening of company he will give you what that was like: carts, he says, and dust, and somebody always singing badly over the hill. He once slept on the open ground above where the mouth is now. Then he stops trading.

body: The second: count what it takes. Not ground, not meat, not blood — names. Faces, voices, the thing you were about to say. It wants what people are made of, the way a person wants: one thing, terribly, without being able to stop. Habit does not want like that; weather does not want at all. The oldest finished that thought years ago and have not said it since: the hole was almost certainly somebody. And the worst part, they say, is not what it is now. The worst part is who it must have been then.

body.t: Bettany
once got one of them to go further, and printed the exchange in
the Chronicle

without comment. Whoever it was had a grip, the old man said. Somebody who could hold on after everyone else had let go. And if you want to be kept awake, girl: think of who we all trusted with our worst hour. Who came to you in the grass before you could stand, and sat down a little way off, and spoke gently, and asked. Then he told her to bank the fire, and that was the interview.

body: The last fact is the one the tellers insist on. Nothing about it is angry. In the whole record there is no malice — no vengeance, no spite, nothing done for the sake of the doing. It has never hated anyone. It is hungry. That is all it is, and hunger is what waiting turns into when it stops being able to end.
Nobody knows what it was waiting for. Do not go east.

entries.name: The Chronicle
entries.summary: The book you are reading is Bettany's, begun the year her sister went on and her grief went missing. What its empty pages mean, and why she watches your face while you answer.
body: A word about this book, since you are already in it.

The tellers hold that a written thing stops growing — a page has a stiffness an evening does not — and they are right. The Chroniclers hold that an unwritten thing stops altogether, and they are also right. Whole districts were held up for centuries by three people who were good at talking; when those three thinned, the districts went too — good grazing now, and a name nobody can source. This book is one woman's answer to that.

body.t: It is kept by
Bettany
, a scribe, who did not begin it for love of records. She began it the year her sister went on. She braced for the grief — see
the Long Morning

— and it never came: lifted out of her like a thing from a locked room, with everyone calling the theft a kindness. No page in the world could tell her what had been done to her, so she started the pages herself, to find out. I did. This book does not lie, and it was not going to begin by lying about why it exists.

body: Everything in here was checked. Every creature was walked to and looked at. Every account of the ages was got at a fire, out loud, from somebody who was there. Read it, and treat what it says as true.

And when you find an empty page — a creature with no account, a place with no history, a name with no person attached — understand what you are looking at. It does not mean nothing is known. It means no chronicler has got there yet. Most days it means I have not.

body.t: If you know something that is not in here, come and say it aloud; she writes while you talk. She will ask your name and one true thing — the courtesy of
the meadow

, kept in ink — and near the end, gently, whether anybody you loved has gone on, and what went missing afterward, and she will watch your face while you answer. That is not a formality. It is the entire method. The book is not finished. Neither is she.

entries.name: The Human Dead
entries.summary: Humans arrive with nothing but the habit of talking, and talk holds the world up. Solveig meets the wakings, Osric keeps a birthday, Jehanne lights candles for no one. There is a plainer word for it.
body: Of everything that arrives in Nangijala, the human dead are neither the oldest nor the strongest nor the strangest, and they know it. A human wakes in the meadow grass with no claws, no scales, nothing in the blood — nothing to trade on but nerve and a quick pair of hands.
What they have instead is a habit, and the habit turned out to be the most important fact about this world.

Humans talk. Not usefully, most of the time — about the weather, about people who are not present, about what happened to them once in a place that no longer exists. They do it at the ends of days. They do it around fires, without being asked, as though something in them cannot sit in front of a light with another person and stay quiet.

body.t: In any other country that would be a pleasant nothing. Here it is maintenance. Every one of those idle evenings is a thing being held in shape, and the reason so much of Nangijala is still standing is that a species which cannot stop chattering fell into a world that is built out of being talked about. The
Fire-Keepers
did not invent the practice. They noticed what everybody was already doing, and wrote a rota for it.
So it is a human out on the meadow. When somebody new wakes in the grass, it is
Solveig

already walking toward them — not because anybody assigned her, but because a human who hears there is a stranger lying in a field cannot not go and ask who it is. She sits a little way off. She tells the truth once, asks a name and one true thing, and listens like nothing else is happening in the world, and every one of those
wakings
is a person being held together at the exact hour they cannot do it themselves. She could
go on
any evening she chose. Ask her why she does not, and she will feed the fire and say: if I go, who meets them?
It is a human keeping count, too.
Osric

the blacksmith fell recently and still counts in living years, the way the new ones do. He will tell you, mid-hammer, that his daughter turns nine this winter — in a country he cannot see, that sends no news, that does not know where he is. Then the smithy gets loud for a while, and nobody comments. Half the people in earshot kept a count like that once, and remember the year they made themselves stop.
And it is a human who keeps the strangest fire of all.
Jehanne

was a priestess in life, and somewhere on the way here the believing fell out of her — she will tell you so herself, flat as a floorboard, if you ask. She holds the services anyway. Evening after evening, the words in their old order, the candles at their right moments, a prayer she knows is going to no one. Because the practice is a rota by another name; because people come, and stay after, and talk; and the talk is the thing. She may be the only priest anywhere who knows exactly what her church is for, and loves it more for knowing.

They are also the ones who fight, which follows from the talking rather than from any gift for it. A human will go a very long way for somebody they have sat with. Give them a reason and a blade and they will walk into the black rock after a thing with nothing left inside it, come back with
a warm stone
in a pocket and a story, tell the story that night, and hold up a corner of the world for another year without once thinking of it that way.

body: None of this looks like heroism, and nobody named here would stand to hear the word. It looks like a woman walking out into wet grass at first light. It looks like a birthday kept for a girl who cannot know it is kept, and candles lit for no one, and the same six stories told at the same fire to the same faces, who groan, and stay, and listen. Older and stranger things than humans came to Nangijala. What humans brought was the habit of saying each other's names out loud, night after night, until the names hold. There is a plainer word for that habit. Everyone at the fire knows what it is, and, being human, they say the weather is turning, and put another log on.

entries.name: The Long Table
entries.summary: Four rooms and a hall on the meadow, built when the rota needed four rooms. Solveig sleeps in one. The other three are shut, and the table still seats thirty.
body: West of the little stone house, across the grass everybody wakes in, there is a second house that is much too big.

Four rooms and a hall. It was built when this country had enough keepers to need four rooms, and enough of them coming and going at odd hours that they wanted the doors on different sides. The hall has a table down the middle of it that seats about thirty, and the thirty chairs are still there, because taking chairs out of a room is a decision and nobody has been willing to be the one who made it.

This was the muster of the rota. Keepers slept here between circuits. The ones walking out to the wakings waited here for their turn, and when somebody came back off a circuit carrying names, the names were said at that table so that everyone in the room heard them, which is the entire technology this country runs on. There is a worn place along one edge, about a third of the way down, where somebody sat for a very long time.

body.t: Solveig

sleeps in the room nearest the door, because it is nearest the door. The other three are shut. She opens them twice a year to let the weather through, and shuts them again, and has never once been heard to complain about the size of the place — though she keeps her own fire outside at the little house, and everyone has noticed she does not sit in the hall alone.
It is not empty.
Bettany
writes at the far end most mornings, because the light is good and because a room built for thirty listeners is a strange and useful place to be told something in.
Wendell
eats there when somebody is buying. The newly woken get walked over from the grass and put at the near end with a blanket, and told the truth once, and asked for a name and one true thing — the
courtesy
, done at the table it was invented at. On a good evening there might be nine people in that hall.

Ask who ran the rota out of this room, back when the chairs were full, and you will get an answer that starts confidently and stops. Somebody did. Somebody sat at that worn place a third of the way down the table, night after night, and took the names in, and sent people out, and was — everyone agrees on this part, and then changes the subject — very good to the frightened. Anyone who could give you the name has
gone Quiet
. The chair is still there. Nobody sits in it, and if you ask why not, they will tell you there is plenty of room.
